description: This module introduces students to the core principles and values that guide contemporary policing practice.  In particular it subjects to critical scrutiny the assertions of the democratic nature of policing with specific focus on the arrangements that seek to ensure the accountability of policing.  Alongside these discussions, the module will consider the impact of human rights norms on contemporary policing practices.

The module will begin with documenting the historical development of contemporary policing practices and arrangements.  In doing so students will be encouraged to consider the shifting model of policing and the social and political factors that have shaped these developments. The module will then be framed around a series of key issues: legitimacy/public opinion; reasonable force; function; and governance.  The module will comprise of contemporary issues: policing and minority ethnic communities; public confidence and policing; counter terrorism policing; deaths in police custody; private forms of policing.

Finally, the module will consider policing models comparatively.  Moreover, students will be introduced to issues in transitional policing and how supra national forms of policing have evolved to meet the challenges of transnational crime.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a critical awareness of the relationship between policing, the media and public perceptions of crime
Identify the principles and values embedded within policing models and the social, political and economic forces that impact policing practices
Critically analyse the rhetoric and reality of policing practice and implementation.
Apply notions of power, democracy, legitimacy, and social justice across a range of contemporary policing issues
Discuss key trends in contemporary policing and identify the similarities and differences evident within domestic and international policing systems
Critically analyse the impact of policing practice in terms of social class, gender and ethnicity

description: Social enterprises are businesses driven by a social mission and put the wellbeing of people and the planet above profit. The proposed module specialises in social enterprise, entrepreneurship and innovation from a social policy perspective. It combines theoretical and practical skills to enable students to understand and explore how social problems could be tackled through enterprise. The module will enable students to design, develop and pitch their own social enterprise proposal.

The module will begin by introducing students to social enterprise as a model that can be used to tackle some of society's most pressing social problems e.g. poverty, unemployment, inequality. Local, national and international perspectives and social enterprise examples will be introduced and critically discussed. Students will be provided with practical entrepreneurial training, which will take them through the processes and pitfalls of setting up a new social enterprise. The module will include creative problem solving through design thinking methodology. It will also support students to develop strategic, project management and business model canvas/presentation skills through interactive lectures, which will support them to confidently pitch their social enterprise to a panel of experts.
The module will engage UK and international social entrepreneurs, as well as Alumni, to support the delivery of specialist workshops and to provide mentoring.

The module assessment will require students to design their own social enterprise to tackle a social problem of their choice. They will be required to write a social enterprise business plan and `pitch? this to a panel of experts.

Build an awareness of the role that social enterprise, entrepreneurship and innovation can play in tackling social problems in the UK and internationally.
Develop the skills to design a social enterprise, pitch the idea and write a business plan.
Understand potential career opportunities through social entrepreneurship, and identify forms of support/funding available in this area.

reassessment: 1000 word written reflection of the group presentation (20%)

description: Housing is one of the most important policy problems facing contemporary governments. This module introduces students to the importance of housing as a key aspect of social policy. description: This module introduces the central ideas of key thinkers in the sociological tradition, as they sought to understand the development of modern industrial societies from the nineteenth century to the 1970s. The module opens with a detailed survey of the three 'founding' thinkers of modern sociology - Marx, Durkheim and Weber, as well as an introduction to those who introduced micro-sociological approaches to the study of everyday life (eg Simmel). The subsequent turning of modern sociological theory against itself, and the emergence of postmodernism, are the starting point for the Level H core module, Contemporary Social Theory.

description: This module will address the role of punishment within contrasting societies as a mechanism for crime control, as well exploring alternative explanations for the social function of punishment. The module will be divided into the following constituent parts:

First, the module will begin with an overview of the historical evolution of punishment, with a particular focus on the shift from capital punishments and transportation to the `birth of the modern prison? in the UK.  Following from the 19th century prison, the module will consider a series of historical policymaking phases, including post-war `penal welfarism? and the recent `prison works? agendas.

Second, the module will consider the varied functions that punishment performs, such as deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation, as well as investigating the liberal philosophies that underpin these ideas.

Third, the module will examine within a comparative context contrasting approaches to punishment, such as Aboriginal/Maori community justice, US `supermax? prisons and Swedish `open? prisons.  Finally, the module will consider contemporary issues in punishment, including mass imprisonment, growth of the penal-security industrial complex, war crimes tribunals and truth and reconciliation commissions.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate an understanding of the historical origins and development of punishment and prisons in the UK and comparative international contexts;
Demonstrate an understanding of the philosophies and aims that underpin punishment;
Discuss comparative and supranational policy approaches to punishment and prison;
To apply concepts and philosophies of punishment to enhance understanding of contemporary policy issues.

description: This module will provide students with an opportunity to critically explore a range of politically salient issues relating to terror, threat and security. Noting the contested nature of how we seek to define terrorism, the module will focus on modern terrorism and the use of terrorist violence to critically consider  a range of key concepts and relevant theories including securitisation and governmentality as also extremism and radicalisation among others. In doing so, consideration will be given to how governments devise and implement appropriate counter-terror policies and approaches as a means of evaluating their effectiveness. The impacts of these will also be explored focusing on notions of suspect communities, social harm, exclusion and marginalisation. From here, students will consider a number of emergent and overarching questions through the lens of a series of case studies to include: terrorist actions perpetrated by state actors; the `war on terror? post-9/11; ethno-nationalist terrorism underpinning conflicts between Israelis and Palestinians and in Northern Ireland; far-right groups and `lone wolf? terrorism; revolutionary left-wing movements; Islamist-inspired terrorism focusing on Islamic State and its activities in both the Middle East and Europe; policing and Project Champion; groups and activists inspired by environmental and vivisection issues; and the role of the media and how it relates to and represents matters of terror, threat and security.

Appraise various policy and legislative approaches relating to counter-terror and security as also extremism and radicalisation
Apply a range of key concepts and theories to the critical investigation of  particular examples of modern terrorism and the use of terrorist violence

description: This module is delivered in two interconnected phases.

The first phase will examine the construction of childhood and youth within political and popular discourse and give consideration to the potential consequences of particular constructions for policy, practice and lived experience. Students will explore the ways in which young people, as a typically marginalised population, are granted or lay claim to agency. Studying 'youth participation' as a policy objective and investigating the unofficial means through which young people may be seen to demonstrate 'voice', students will consider and critique the positioning of young people within society.

Focusing upon the construction of 'troublesome youth', the second phase of the module will explore the current and historical concern with youth and crime. Students will explore the theoretical analyses and policy responses to 'at risk' youth. Supported through a comparative perspective, the module will examine the ways in which understanding of, and responses to 'youth crime', differ across national boundaries; challenging the doxa of dominant approaches. The module will conclude by investigating possible explanations for convergence and divergence in youth justice policy and practice, and considering opportunities for future policy development.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate an understanding of the variety of ways that 'childhood' and 'youth' may be constructed and its intersection with notions of class, gender, and ethnicity
Critically evaluate the construction of 'youth' within political and policy discourses
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the historical and contemporary concern with youth and crime
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the key principles and theoretical frameworks which guide policy and practice response to youth crime

description: The module develops student understanding of social research in practice, across the research process. There is a focus on developing a working knowledge of a range of approaches for analysing and handling data through engagement with large-scale secondary research.  The teaching and assessment engages with the overall process of research through examining the means through which data is constructed, drawing on relevant records of the research process which lie behind the data accessed during this course. The module includes a number of statistical approaches to handling and analysing survey/numeric data, and rigorous approaches to analysing qualitative data.  Important topics will include how to balance analysing according to a plan (or theory) while allowing ideas to emerge from the evidence, the role of judgement in all analysis, and thus the importance of transparently reporting all research decisions (and other good practice in handling data) to facilitate `replication?.For analysing large-scale survey data, the emphasis is on developing an adequate understanding of statistical principles, descriptive and exploratory methods of analysis (especially graphical methods), operational procedures and interpretations of outputs from statistical packages (SPSS, in this course). description: This is a broad module covering a range of contemporary issues and debates relating to crime, justice and punishment in the UK and internationally, which will be taught by experts in those areas.

The module will begin with a brief overview of main theories of punishment, drawing attention to current academic and policy debates around these theories. It will then consider how approaches to punishment developed in Western societies (eg. UK, EU countries and USA, but not limited to there).

The module will consider ongoing debates about the criminal justice system in the context of specific groups of people who offend. These debates will be explored in relation to gender, age, 'race' and ethnicity and socioeconomic background. It will also consider the ongoing international trend towards the abolition of the death penalty. Furthermore, students will be invited to explore the proliferation of innovative approaches to punishment, such as restorative justice and specialist courts (eg. drug courts, mental health courts).

Finally, the growing and changing roles of mass and social media in reporting crime and shaping/influencing public opinion and policy around crime and punishment will be considered. The increasing politicisation of crime and justice discourse will be focussed on, as well as concepts such as popular punitivism and 'othering' of specific groups.

outcomes.outcome: Critically analyse and synthesise information about a range of theories of punishment.
Demonstrate a contemporary understanding of the evolution of approaches to punishing crime within Western democracies.
Assess, analyse and propose solutions to contemporary punishment debates in the context of race, class, gender, and age.
Showcase a deep understanding of the evolving nature of debates within punishment and society and the socio-political and media factors that drive them.

summative: Policy brief focussing on a contemporary issue to be chosen from a range of options - 4,000 words.

description: From megadroughts and sea level rise to heatwaves, wildfires and species loss, climate change affects us all. However, the felt impacts of climate change, and climate policies, are unevenly distributed along the lines of race, class, gender, and ethnicity, with growing recognition that increased convergence between social and environmental policy is essential to achieving equitable climate action. This module explores some of the key conceptual and analytical issues in the study of climate justice, examining how global climate change both emerges from and reinforces historically inequitable power relations. It also explores the intersections between climate change and the various domains of social policy, recognising that the climate crisis requires a whole systems, multisectoral response. Contemporary case studies are drawn from countries across the globe to illustrate these key debates, with an emphasis on historically marginalised communities.

Identify and evaluate key analytical issues in debates concerning climate justice and social policy
Have knowledge of the ways in which climate impacts are felt unevenly across different groups
Critically apply these debates to substantive case studies on the climate crisis

description: For more than four decades, the UK has seen a retrenchment of welfare provision and radical changes in the balance of responsibilities between the state, business, and households. Alongside this shift, current global economic shocks, such as the pandemic, have led households to face more financial uncertainty/precarity due to the cost-of-living crisis. Despite these developments, achieving financial well-being and inclusion is highly crucial and is linked to effective policy approaches and responses. This module explores key conceptual and policy debates on financial well-being and inclusion by delving into issues including the impact of social policy on financial well-being, financial choices, and behaviours across different stages of life course and population groups with a focus on marginalised communities. This study will engage with national and international evidence and contemporary examples on work patterns and earnings, savings and debts, social security, health, intergenerational aspects of family, and financial well-being to illustrate these key concepts and debates.

description: This module will explore theories surrounding the intersection of migration, citizenship and globalisation. It offers a critical overview of academic scholarship in migration studies paying particular attention to the policies and politics that shape responses to migration at international, EU, national, and local levels.  It will challenge students to think critically about migration and the impact upon public policy and to examine reactions and responses to migration from a range of contrasting perspectives.

This module will enrich the offer on the MA in Migration, Superdiversity and Policy providing an advanced module in which to explore in greater depth the intersections of policy, international migration and societal transformation. The MA in Migration currently includes only one migration-related module. In the current programme issues of migration are touched upon but mainly addressed in relation to new migration and within the national context. This module places the relationship between migration and citizenship at its core and explores shifting understanding of belonging in Western liberal democracies as well as in new immigration hubs. It explores the impact of this relationship on ideas of deservingness, entitlement and access to public services and social welfare.

It is critical that our MA in Migration and other MA programmes offer module options that reflect both cutting-edge academic debates as well as policy and legislative developments in this area. Given its global scope, the proposed module will also enhance our MA offer to international students and further enrich the study offer for students who come to the University of Birmingham, located within one of the most multicultural cities in the UK, to learn about all aspects of Social Policy including diversity and migration. It would provide an advanced option on migration issues for the MA in Global Social Policy currently under discussion.

The module is likely to be of interest to students enrolled on programmes in other departments across the University e.g. Sociology, Social Psychology, Planning, History, Law, Politics, Human Geography. The module leader and the Director of the MA have had numerous conversations with key contacts in other departments, particularly those linked to the Institute for Research into Superdiversity. and are currently finalising a list of MA programmes where the course will be offered as a MOMD.

outcomes.outcome: Critically evaluate the relationship between globalisation, international migration and approaches to migration governance;
Critically analyse the ways in which international migration shapes and is shaped by different understandings of citizenship and belonging;
Critically discuss the intersections of different level of governance in policy and practice related to international migration, integration and social inclusion;
Demonstrate self direction and originality in tackling course tasks and the module assessment.

reassessment: 1000 word written reflection of the group presentation (20%)

description: Causality plays a central role in both empirical and theoretical research however, causal effects are difficult to establish. Especially when working with observational data, researchers miss crucial information for making causal interpretations of statistical associations. This module explores general approaches to studying causality in the social sciences, including through experimental, observational, and simulation-based designs. It provides and overview of key research designs and modern methods of causal inference for social sciences research. The module discusses theories of causality, the potential outcome framework, the fundamental problem of causal inference, and suitable causal identification strategies. Students can develop their skills of analysing causal links through empirical examples presented using the R programming language.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and critically discuss key approaches to establishing causal links in the social sciences.
Represent complex causal links between phenomena using causal graphs.
Interpret empirical results from research designs aimed at causal inference.
Carry out simple analysis aimed at causal inference. using the R programming language.
Summarise findings from their data analysis using appropriate causal language.

summative: A 2,000-word written report on a small data analysis project (100%)

description: This module introduces students to a range of ?typical? welfare ideologies before introducing a range of critical perspectives. The aim is to provide a firm grounding in key theoretical debates which inform the development and critique of welfare provision in the UK (and beyond).

The module starts with an exploration of conservativism, liberalism and social democracy before examining contemporary forms of neo-liberalism and the third way. Attention then moves on to examine critical theories: Marxism, Feminism and Anti-racism as traditional points of critique before examining new points of departure in relation to environmentalism, anarchy, queer theory, morality and temporality.

Exploration of each philosophy examines its key frameworks, its relevance to concepts of need, citizenship, social rights and social justice before illustrating the application of these in the forms of welfare system and society pursued through their implementation. Thus, the module seeks to explore with students how philosophical and theoretical debates are played out in policy practice.

description: This module introduces students to the work of Stuart Hall and cultural studies, it encourages interdisciplinary discussion and debate and is suitable for students taking social sciences, humanities and arts courses.

Born in Jamaica in 1932, Hall came to Britain in 1951 becoming one of the most significant public intellectuals of the twentieth century. Frequently cited across social science and humanities disciplines, Hall was central to establishing the field of cultural studies, and made significant interventions in cultural and political life in Britain and internationally.

Students will be introduced to key concepts, methods, and arguments in Hall's work - including his interdisciplinary and collaborative research methods, media analysis, histories and theory of crime and deviancy, concepts of class and 'race', political and state theory, and theories of social and cultural formation and change. Using major works by Hall and his colleagues at the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, students will be given the opportunity to develop interpretative and analytical skills and given instruction and guided access to the use of the Stuart Hall Archive and other national and international resources for understanding Hall's distinctive approach to cultural studies. Students completing the module will have a clear understanding of Hall's life and work and be able to apply this to their own academic, cultural, and political interests.

outcomes.outcome: Critically evaluate competing historic and contemporary interpretations of Stuart Hall's work
Systematically review and utilise qualitative empirical sources
Critically reflect on ethical and epistemological assumptions derived from disciplinary and social formation
Design an inter-disciplinary research proposal

reassessment: 40% Individual Recorded Presentation (10 mins) OR Individual Written Assignment (1,500 words)

The module is underpinned by practical case studies from a variety of policy areas, such as health, housing and migration, from a range of global contexts. Overall, The module will provide the student with an opportunity to develop and refine a range of transferable skills in policy analysis and communication.

outcomes.outcome: Critically discuss the nature and role of policy analysis.
Understanding of policymaking processes in different international contexts
Demonstrate an understanding of the theories and methods of comparative policy analysis, and use these to analyse a policy issue across multiple countries

description: Addressing issues of poverty and inequality are pressing social and political issues of our time.   This module will explore different approaches to the definition and measurement of poverty and inequality and their implications for our understanding of the scale and drivers of disadvantage.  These ideas will be illuminated through discussion of a variety of issues, including citizenship/human rights, age, disability, gender, and ethnicity, as well as policy areas, namely health, housing and crime.  Students will be challenged to consider a range of theories and methodological approaches used to research this area and their relationship to effective evidence-based policies.  Throughout the module the emphasis is upon understanding the relationship between empirical research and anti-poverty policy, as well as how policy might best address the issue of widening inequality and its consequences.

description: Sociology has been looking at race and racism since the second half of the 19th century. The aim of this module is the critical understanding of race as one of the most deep-rooted principles organizing both the material and the symbolic structures of society in hierarchies of moral worth. Racism, as coterminous and direct extension of race, will be scrutinized in its most evident manifestations, from everyday contingencies to socio-spatial urban inequalities, textured by global capitalism. Race and racism will be presented and discussed from a historical and comparative sociological perspective, detecting both a comprehensive genealogy of racism across various imperial colonial projects, and the key and intersectional forms of racist exclusion within dominant manifestations of contemporary neoliberalism (e.g. recent global wars; the financialization of the economy, and the pluralization and privatization of detention).

The module starts with a theoretical and historical overview of race and racism, and continues with a series of specific themes including ?The racial state?; ?Everyday racism?; ?Racism and the city?, ?Intersectionality?, and ?(Post-)Race, racism and neoliberalism?.   Parallel to these emphases runs an in-depth examination of European colonialism, which is developed in every class by watching and discussing a brief excerpt of the 3-hour BBC documentary "Racism: A history" (2007), directed by Paul Tickell. Europe as a historical and sociological formation will be a privileged focus throughout.

The module is organized neither as a structured lecture series nor as a free-floating seminar. Rather, at the beginning of each class the lecturer will provide a background summary of the theme, before starting a collective discussion. You are not expected to already have knowledge on the subject, but only background knowledge in any of the social sciences and the readiness to read and engage in discussions. Two readings per class are mandatory, and optional readings will be suggested. You will be asked to initiate discussions on the readings by bringing to the group your critical question(s).

outcomes.outcome: Form a theoretically and historically grounded understanding of the main ways in which race and racism operate
Outline and critically discuss different dimensions of inequalities, including class, gender and race in understanding different social structures and agencies
Being able to critically deconstruct generalizations from specific racist manifestations to grand pictures, and to gain the ability of dissecting the contextual specificities of racism

Critically analyse and recognize the modalities of oblivion, neglect and denial of race, especially in post-WWII Europe, and yet to understand why many of us have a hard time accepting the centrality of race in society
Critically analyse and historicize the making of Europe as a hegemonic global power
Form a solid, contextualized and critical understanding of the ways in which racism can be opposed, both in theory and in practice

description: This module critically examines how our individual and collective identities are shaped by and constitute wider processes of social change. It charts the contribution social theory has made to our understanding of the self and identity, and how identities are implicated in both social change and reproduction. The contestation and negotiation of identity is explored in key contemporary social settings such as debates over body technology and post-humanism; gender, ethnic and sexual identity; personal relationships; self-help and self-optimisation;  new political subjectivities, ideology and discourse; the role of mass and niche media, culture and consumption.

outcomes.outcome: Draw on classic and contemporary social theory - and allied disciplines ? to critically interrogate the nature of human identity
Identify key transitions in the nature of identity construction in contemporary societies
Understand identity as both constitutive of and constituted by wider social structures and relations
Critically analyse processes of identity formation in key substantive areas of contemporary social life
Understand identity as a crucial contemporary site of power, political contestation and social transformation

description: This module critically examines the key structural shifts that are shaping the trajectory of contemporary societies. It integrates material from classic and contemporary social theory, and applies them to substantive and empirical areas such as the nature of cultural and economic globalisation; the social impact of new technologies; social divisions and social power; the rise of new forms of populism and social activism; and changes in the structure of key institutions such as work, consumption and democracy. It explores the role of the sociological imagination in both understanding and critically intervening in these processes.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and explain the key macro social transformations that characterise contemporary societies
Draw on classic and contemporary social theory to critically interrogate these transformations in terms of e.g. power relations; forms of social stratification and inequality

Develop a critical understanding of the interplay between key analytical categories such as  the global/local, structure/agency, stability/change, and material/cultural in driving societal transformation
Apply these ideas to substantive areas that exemplify contemporary transformations
Understand societal transformation as a contested field in which critical sociological knowledge can make key interventions and envisage alternatives

This will include not only British Sign Language but also non-verbal and written communication. The module will also consider effective ways to assess the needs of D/deaf people with mental health problems.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and describe a range of effective communication methods for interaction with D/deaf people.
Recognise factors that can help/hinder effective communication with D/deaf people.
Describe factors to consider in the informal assessment of D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Describe formal approaches to needs assessment of D/deaf people with mental health problems.

data.title: LC Deaf and Mental Health Awareness
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module aims to introduce students to basic deaf awareness including issues of culture, communication and access to services. The module will also examine mental health issues as experienced by D/deaf people and the availability of specialist and generic health and social services. Central to this awareness raising will be an understanding of how multiple forms of discrimination and oppression related to deafness and mental health intertwine to create disadvantage and exclusion and what can be done to challenge this oppression/discrimination.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the kinds barriers D/deaf people experience in everyday life and access to services.
Identify the factors important to consider when interacting and communicating with D/deaf people.
Describe the diversity existing within the deaf population.
Identify the range of mental health problems experienced by D/deaf people.
Describe the range of specialist and generic services and interventions available for D/deaf people with Mental Health problems

data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module aims to introduce the students to psychologically informed theory and interventions for understanding the life-span development of D/deaf people and the potential risk factors for developing mental health problems. This module will also examine what, from a psychological and developmental perspective, can act to protect and enhance positive mental health for D/deaf people.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and describe the basic tenets of behaviourism and their relevance to D/deaf people.
Understand processes of socialisation for D/deaf people.
Describe the use of psychological interventions (Behavioural Modification; Cognitive Approaches; Psychodynamic Interventions) for D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Describe and differentiate a range of developmental perspectives relevant to understanding the life-span of D/deaf people.
Describe the difference between typical, delayed and atypical development for D/deaf people.
Describe and understand a range of developmental risk factors for mental health problems in D/deaf people

summative: 750 word description of the potential developmental factors from early life that may result in mental health difficulties for a D.deaf person (50%) + a 750 word case example of how psychological interventions (e.g. cognitive; psychodynamic) may usefully be incorporated into a D/deaf person with mental health problems care plan (50%)

This module supports students' preparation for the first period of practice learning.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate self-awareness and apply critical analysis to the use of self in communication and appreciate how one's own personal values can impact on others and social work practice.
Develop verbal, non-verbal, written, group work, presentation, assertiveness, and conflict resolution skills both through face-to-face and online communication skills.
Exercise the ability to listen actively to others and communicate effectively across potential barriers resulting from issues of power and inequality.
Demonstrate an understanding of the application of relevant theories and models and skills of critical reflection.

description: This introductory module is designed with reference to the Code of Practice on Personal Academic Tutoring to support students to make a successful transition from previous study or work to higher education and specifically education and training in qualifying professional social work.

Students will be introduced to core skills for academic learning and strategies for developing those skills. The focus will be on critical thinking, reflective social work practice and effective communication for academic and professional audiences with reference to the relevant professional standards.
Students will be introduced to a range of approaches to collaborative and independent learning in preparation for work throughout the programme.
The module is designed to foster positive peer relationships within the cohort in preparation for their work together during the rest of the programme.

outcomes.outcome: Understand and practise the skills associated with sourcing, accessing, and organising resources for learning and practice.

Demonstrate ability to take responsibility for own learning by understanding the importance of individual needs and be able to recognise and identify their own needs in both the academic and professional context as well as be empathic to the needs of others.

Demonstrate ability to work collegially by understanding the principles and practice of the skills necessary for communicating effectively with a range of different audiences including academic, professionals and service users & carers.

description: This module offers a general consideration of the English legal system focusing on specific legislative frameworks, policies, and guidance for social work practice with a variety of service users.

It highlights the key ethical principles and theories that underpin the law and the professional social work mandates that these principles inform including social work values, policy and practice frameworks, organisational and multi-agency requirements, and human rights and equalities provisions.

The module enables students to develop the ability to apply law to social work problems including those pertaining to state intervention, risk, harm, autonomy, protection, safeguarding, rights, personalisation, and wellbeing.
The module emphasises the necessity for practitioners to be confident when representing agencies and working with service users in various legislative contexts.

outcomes.outcome: Understand the principles of human and civil rights and equalities legislation and how to promote individuals' rights to autonomy and self-determination
Understand the basis of the English Legal System, and the place of social work within it, including key parts of primary and secondary legislation.
Demonstrate knowledge of how the law can be applied in direct social work practice taking account of the principles of social justice, inclusion, and equality
Analyse ways in which use of the law can create ethical dilemmas and lead to issues of oppression and discrimination and how this can be managed.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the role and responsibilities of a social worker in training and evidence working towards Social Work England's professional standards in readiness for their application for registration.
Articulate the values and ethics of social work, understand its ethical basis and the potential dilemmas involved in professional practice
To recognise diversity and apply anti-discriminatory, anti-oppressive and anti-racist principles in practice
Demonstrate effective interpersonal and communication skills and an ability to apply an initial understanding of critical reflection and analysis.

Pass in Readiness to Practice (PRSB requirement)

description: This module will introduce students to a range of social work theories, models, and methods of practice within the context of the Professional Capabilities Framework for Social Work and the Knowledge and Skills Statements for Social Work. The module seeks to develop the theoretical learning that is needed to practice reflectively and effectively by examining contemporary practice models to develop understanding of the place of theory and evidence in social work in guiding and evaluating assessments and interventions.
It will enable students to explore and evaluate these interventions within the principles of anti -oppressive practice and from the perspective of social work agencies, social work
practitioners, other professionals, and service users and carers.
The module seeks to equip students to develop theoretical knowledge and skills for their first social work placement and contributes to the 30 days skills development requirement.

Demonstrate the ability to apply a range of social work theories and methods in the context of working with children, young people and adults who are service users or carers.
Compare social work theories, models, and methods from the perspectives of practitioners, other professionals, service users and carers.
Distinguish between different social work theories, perspectives, models, and methods of intervention within the context of professional values and inter-professional practice.

Recognise and describe the main types of abuse D/deaf people with mental health problems may experience.

data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
coreqs: 08 21708 LC Soc Contexts for Soc Work
data.restrictions: For students on BA Social Work programme
description: It is important for students intending to work with and for the most vulnerable members of society to develop a critical understanding of the part society and social policy play in creating and framing the problems that people face. A failure to develop an understanding of this can lead students to respond to social problems as problems with individuals, which itself can be problematic. A range of sociological and social policy perspectives and methodological approaches are available to help make sense of the social issues faced by people who may be using social care services.

This module explores the relationship between social problems, social policy and social work intervention in contemporary society  through a series of 5 case studies on various topics of current interest, for example poverty, migration and health.

outcomes.outcome: Understand the complex nature of social issues and recognise connections between daily experiences and larger social forces.
Identify, understand and critically explore the contested nature of policy interventions.
Understand the significance of rights, justice and economic wellbeing for social policy and social work practice
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of social policy on people's lives.
Demonstrate they understand and are working towards Social Work England's professional standards in readiness for their application for registration.

summative: 3000 word assignment for main and reassessment (100%)

data.title: LC Social Perspectives on Mental Health and Deafness
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: The module aims to explore relationships between social characteristics and patterns of mental distress; introduce theoretical ideas about both the social construction and social creation of mental illness; and in particular explore how they impact upon the experiences D/deaf people have of mental distress. It will also review the role of social interventions in facilitating the recovery of D/deaf people experiencing mental distress.

outcomes.outcome: Outline what is meant by the social construction and social creation of mental illness.
Identify the positive and negative consequences of labelling.
Describe the role of power in the origins of mental distress and the particular role this plays in the mental distress of D/deaf people.
Identify and describe social interventions appropriate to work with D/deaf people experiencing mental distress.

data.title: LC Social, Political and Organisational Context for Social Work
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 5641 - BA Social Work FT
980C - BA Social Work w Yr Ab FT

description: This module will provide students with an understanding of the historical and contemporary context of social work in relation to national and international models of welfare, concepts of human need, theories of power and society, and social and health inequalities.

These insights require professionals working in the field of social work to develop an appreciation of the social construction of social problems as well as the social material determinants of wellbeing across the life course.

There will be a specific focus on social divisions in society to enable and examination of the ways in which inequality, discrimination and oppression manifest themselves in society, and impact on the provision and organisation of social work services.
The global context of local social work practice ('glocal') and the way an understanding of this informs a commitment to decolonising the agenda and anti-oppressive practice will also be addressed.

outcomes.outcome: 1. Describe the historical development of social work and demonstrate an understanding of different helping professions and how social work is distinguished from them.
2. Understand the impact of economic, social, political, and organisational developments in the provision of social work.
3. Analyse key theories and concepts that inform social policy and contemporary social work contexts.

4. Understand the nature of social divisions in society and demonstrate an awareness of the ways in which the policies, procedures and practices can operate an oppressive manner thus the need to commit to a decolonising and anti-discrimination agenda.

reassessment: Individual reassessment for group presentation through a short reflective commentary. 500 words (20%)

data.title: LC The Legal, Policy and Values Framework for Mental Health & Deafness
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: The focus of this module is the legal, policy and values framework for mental health service provision for D/deaf people. The students will be introduced to the 10 Essential Shared Capabilities and how a Values Based Practice approach can help to understand and implement positive values from a deaf perspective. Identify and describe the 10 Essential Shared Capabilities from a deaf perspective.
Identify the key contents of the legal and policy framework for mental health and deafness.
Describe and evaluate how the legal and policy framework for mental health and deafness helps shape access and service provision for D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Describe the roles and responsibilities created for practitioners working with D/deaf people with mental health problems by the legal and policy framework.

Contribute to supporting the learning and development of others.

This will include not only British Sign Language but also non-verbal and written communication. outcomes.outcome: Evaluate a range of effective communication methods for interaction with D/deaf people.
Critically examine factors that can help/hinder effective communication with D/deaf people.
Critically identify factors to consider in the informal assessment of D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Evaluate formal approaches to needs assessment of D/deaf people with mental health problems.

data.title: LH Consolidating Social Care Practice with Adults
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 7199 - BPhil SpecSocWorkAdults (Flex)

data.restrictions: BPhil In Specialist Social Work with Adults, Undergraduate Affiliate in Specialist Social Work with Adults
description: This module offers a structured opportunity for candidates to take stock of, and reflect on, their knowledge, values and skills relevant to practice in the adult social care sector - and how they have developed this since initial qualification.  It is designed to facilitate demonstration that candidates are operating within the specialist adults context at the `social worker? level of the Professional Capabilities Framework (PCF). It may be taken as an individual module for candidates who are not able to take the time out of their role to complete a full programme. It also acts as an entry module for candidates working towards the PG Diploma in Specialist Social Work with Adults as they progress to the PCF's "experienced social worker level".

outcomes.outcome: Reflect upon and evaluate the effectiveness of their post-qualifying practice using a relevant knowledge base, including an understanding of legal and policy contexts and appropriate research;
Describe and analyse the application of the values of social work and the principles of ethical practice in their post-qualifying social work practice with adults;
Identify and evaluate the impact of social work interventions with adults based upon a range of different models of intervention.

summative: An analytical case study of 3000 words (100% of mark);Report on direct observation of the candidate's practice and 1000 word analysis of the practice completed by the candidate (Pass / fail).

data.title: LH Deaf and Mental Health Awareness (Advanced)
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module aims to introduce students to basic deaf awareness including issues of culture, communication and access to services. The module will also examine mental health issues as experienced by D/deaf people and the availability of specialist and generic health and social services. Central to this awareness raising will be an understanding of how multiple forms of discrimination and oppression related to deafness and mental health intertwine to create disadvantage and exclusion and what can be done to challenge this oppression/discrimination.

outcomes.outcome: Critically evaluate the kinds of barriers D/deaf people experience in everyday life and access to services.
Critically assess the key factors important that it is important to consider when interacting and communicating with D/deaf people.
Describe the diversity within the deaf population and critically examine the potential for multiple discrimination and oppression.
Demonstrate an understanding of mental health problems from a D/deaf person's perspective.
Describe the range of specialist and generic services and interventions available for D/deaf people with Mental Health problems and critically examine issues of access.

data.title: LH Developmental and Psychological Perspectives on Mental Health & Deafness (Advanced)
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module aims to introduce the students to psychologically informed theory and interventions for understanding the life-span development of D/deaf people and the potential risk factors for developing mental health problems. This module will also examine what, from a psychological and developmental perspective, can act to protect and enhance positive mental health for D/deaf people.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the basic tenets of behaviourism and their relevance to D/deaf people.
Critically examine processes of socialisation for D/deaf people.
Evaluate the use of psychological interventions (Behavioural Modification; Cognitive Approaches; Psychodynamic Interventions) with D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Describe a range of developmental perspectives relevant to understanding the life-span of D/deaf people.
Evaluate the difference between typical, delayed and atypical development for D/deaf people.
Critically examine a range of developmental risk factors for mental health problems in D/deaf people.

data.title: LH Developments in the Legislative Framework and Social Care Practice with Adults
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

optional: 7199 - BPhil SpecSocWorkAdults (Flex)

data.restrictions: BPhil In Specialist Social Work with Adults, Undergraduate Affiliate in Specialist Social Work with Adults.
description: This module assumes a basic knowledge of community care law and builds on that foundation by exploring and assessing the impact of recent changes in community care legislation and policy, case law and mental health legislation. The use of legislation in practice to empower and protect adults will also be explored.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and apply in practice legislation relevant to adult protection work;
Identify and reflect on the implications for social work practice with adults of case law and the Human Rights Act;
Describe and evaluate how the principles concerning capacity and consent enshrined within mental health and other legislation may be applied in relation to social care practice with adults.

data.title: LH Dissertation A
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 5641 - BA Social Work FT
980C - BA Social Work w Yr Ab FT

data.restrictions: Compulsory for all BA Social Work Students
description: This module is designed to provide opportunities for students to develop and apply the research skills necessary for critical evidence based practice. It allows for the summative assessment of the process of the design and undertaking of a research project, through the requirement to complete various guided activities and to include those as appendices to the assignment. This more structured approach will strengthen the learning experience for the students, support repeated use in future professional contexts, and necessarily reflect the work required.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a critical understanding of research methods;
Demonstrate a critical awareness of current issues within social work and recognise the potential contribution of research to inform practice and decision making;
Demonstrate advanced conceptual understanding in translating broad topic interests into coherent research questions;
Identify and develop appropriate methods for identifying and accessing literature based data, gathering information from a variety of sources;
Take responsibility for managing your time and workload effectively, and begin to prioritise your activity including supervision time.
Demonstrate they understand and are working towards Social Work England's professional standards in readiness for their application for registration.

summative: Assessments: 6,000 (max) word research protocol, and associated documentation outlining the background, purpose and search strategy for a literature based dissertation.

data.title: LH Dissertation B
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 5641 - BA Social Work FT
980C - BA Social Work w Yr Ab FT

data.restrictions: Compulsory for all BA Social Work Students
description: This module is designed to provide opportunities for students to develop and apply the research skills necessary for critical evidence based practice with added emphasis on the translation of research findings into recommendations for policy and practice - a key intended outcome of the research process.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a critical understanding of research methods;
In developing a framework for analysis, demonstrate advanced conceptual understanding and apply this to the findings from their research;

In presenting their findings, demonstrate their ability to critically evaluate current research and scholarship within social work, question its reliability and validity, and review hypotheses in response to available evidence;
Consider recommendations for policy and/or practice from their research;
Take responsibility for managing your time and workload effectively, and begin to prioritise your activity including supervision time.
Demonstrate they understand and are working towards Social Work England's professional standards in readiness for their application for registration.

summative: Assessments: 6,000 words maximum research report, including recommendations for policy and/or practice.

data.title: LH Dissertation Study
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module gives students the opportunity to engage in a substantial piece of individual research and/or practice development work, focussed on a topic that is of interest to them.

The module enables students to plan and conduct an in-depth piece of research on a topic that contributes to professional social work practice. The chosen topic will require students to identify/formulate problems and issues, conduct literature reviews, evaluate information, investigate, and adopt suitable research methodologies in drawing conclusions and making recommendations.

outcomes.outcome: 1.Explain the different approaches and methods commonly used in social work research.
2.Design and undertake a critical analysis of research.
3.Interrogate a review of the research literature on their chosen topic, informed by systematic review principles and methods including an appraisal of the quality of research evidence.
4. Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of research on a specific aspect of social work and its relevance to social work practice.

reassessment: Re-assessment by failed component where a student has failed to pass the module at the first attempt.

data.title: LH Engagement and Support in Working with Carers in Social Care Practice with Adults
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

optional: 7199 - BPhil SpecSocWorkAdults (Flex)

data.restrictions: BPhil In Specialist Social Work with Adults, Undergraduate Affiliate in Specialist Social Work with Adults.
description: This module explores how to work collaboratively with carers as part of delivering a social work service to vulnerable adult service users - including a focus on legislative and policy context, social work skills and underpinning values.

outcomes.outcome: By the end of this module the student should be able to:
Demonstrate understanding of a range of theoretical ideas underpinning work with carers;
Demonstrate skills in engaging with and supporting carers;
Demonstrate application of understanding of the policy and legislation directly relevant to work with carers in the context of social work with adults;
Demonstrate application of the principles of Anti-Discriminatory Practice within interventions with carers.

summative: 3000 word case study (100% of mark);Report on direct observation of the candidate's practice and satisfactory feedback from a carer (pass / fail).

data.title: LH Legal, Policy and Values Framework for Mental Health & Deafness (Advanced)
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: The focus of this module is the legal, policy and values framework for mental health service provision for D/deaf people. The students will be introduced to the 10 Essential Shared Capabilities and how a Values Based Practice approach can help to understand and implement positive values from a deaf perspective. The module will also critically examine the interaction of deaf specific and generic mental health law and policy on the lives of D/deaf people with mental health problems as well as the key roles and responsibilities for practitioners that this legal and policy framework creates.

outcomes.outcome: Critically examine the role of a Values Based Practice approach in mental health and deafness service provision.
Evaluate the 10 Essential Shared Capabilities from a deaf perspective.
Identify the key contents of the legal and policy framework for mental health and deafness.
Examine critically how the legal and policy framework for mental health and deafness helps shape access and service provision for D/deaf people with mental health problems.
Evaluate the roles and responsibilities created for practitioners working with D/deaf people with mental health problems by the legal and policy framework.

data.title: LH Placement 2
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 5641 - BA Social Work FT
980C - BA Social Work w Yr Ab FT

data.restrictions: Only open to students registered on BA Social Work
description: This module builds on learning undertaken in Placement 1 (08 25947) and Enhancing Skills for Social Work Practice (08 25946) modules in Year 2, and Advanced practice: Individuals, Families, Communities module in Year 3. It moves the student on into an advanced practice placement in a social work agency. The module will allow students to build their practice experience in statutory social work tasks and apply legislation to their work. They will continue to build their understanding and apply theories and methods that underpin social work practice. There continue to be a particular focus on incorporating and learning from the perspectives of service users and carers in undertaking processes of assessment and in the planning and delivery of social work support and intervention.

outcomes.outcome: Meet the assessment requirements for The HCPC Standards of Proficiency and PCF `End of Last Placement/Qualifying level?;

Demonstrate professionalism in their behaviour with others (service users, colleagues both within and external to the placement agency) and in relation to self (taking responsibility for their own safety and wellbeing);
Apply social work values in practice; identify and manage value tensions and conflicts and demonstrate respectful partnership with others;

Demonstrate the ability to work with people from diverse backgrounds taking account of the impact of discrimination, oppression and poverty, and the power invested in the social work role - and use a range of approaches to enhance people's rights, opportunities and wellbeing;

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the application to social work of research, theory and knowledge from sociology, social policy, psychology and health and of the legal and policy frameworks and guidance that inform and mandate social work practice, recognising the scope for professional judgement and the limits of own understanding;
Demonstrate a holistic approach to the identification of needs, circumstances, rights, strengths and risks, and identify the factors that may create or exacerbate risk;

Demonstrate the ability to apply critical reflection to practice and inform own decision-making through the identification and gathering of information from multiple sources. Show ability to question and evaluate the reliability and validity of information from different sources and use this to begin to make evidence-informed judgements and justifiable decisions;

Understand the roles and responsibilities of social workers and be able to work within lines of accountability and the organisations remit. Understand the importance of inter-agency working and demonstrate the ability to undertake effective partnership working;
Contribute to the learning and development of others including social work colleagues, service users and carers, volunteers, foster carers and other professionals.
Demonstrate they understand and are working towards Social Work England's professional standards in readiness for their application for registration.

summative: The module learning will be assessed both academically and professionally. Students will compile a portfolio of practice-based evidence during the placement.
Academic assessment will be based on a practice analysis (3500-4000 words), submitted as part of the practice portfolio. This will constitute 100% of the academic credits.

Professional assessment will be based on evaluation by qualified and experienced social work practice educators of the student's performance in practice and the evidence contained in the practice portfolio. Professional assessment will be based on the Professional Capabilities Framework requirements. The professional assessment will be Pass/Fail and this will constitute an internal hurdle.
To be awarded credits for the module and proceed, students must pass both the academic and professional components of assessment.
reassessment: Reassessment of the academic work will require resubmission of the practice analysis.
Reassessment of the professional component will be decided on the basis of an Independent Practice Assessor investigation and report, as specified in the Course Approval documentation.

data.title: LH Placement Two for Professional Practice
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module builds on learning undertaken in Placement One acquiring the relevant professional knowledge, skills and behaviours required at qualifying level. Students will also gain an understanding of the role of the KSS as a framework for post-qualifying practice, in preparation for future employment.

The module will allow students to build their practice experience in social work tasks and apply legislation to their work. They will continue to build their understanding and apply theories and methods that underpin social work practice. There will continue to be a particular focus on incorporating and learning from the perspectives of service users and carers in undertaking processes of assessment and in the planning and delivery of social work support and intervention.

Students will be equipped with the skills to apply for employment opportunities and understand their obligations and opportunities in relation to Continuous Professional Development. Including an understanding of the Social Work Knowledge and Skills Statements (KSS) with which they will be assessed once in employment.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate professionalism in their behaviour with others (service users, colleagues both within and external to the placement agency) and in relation to self (taking responsibility for their own safety and wellbeing).
Apply a range of social work practice theory in a critically reflective way.
Demonstrate a critically reflective understanding of self in relation to being a social work practitioner including constructive use of feedback.
Demonstrate competence in social work practice against End of Final Placement level.
Critically analyse the concept of the reflective practitioner and its relationship to evidence-based practice and the research informed practitioner.
Critically reflect on the place of social work in organisational structures and the tensions and issues in contemporary social work practice.
Critically evaluate their duties and obligations as professional social workers in relation to the Professional Capabilities Framework, SWE Professional standards and SWE expectations of Registrants.

summative: The professional assessment (placement) will be Pass/Fail and this will constitute an internal hurdle.
To be awarded credits for the module and proceed, students must pass both the academic and professional components of assessment.
reassessment: Re-assessment by failed component with normally one opportunity to re-take the placement unless a student is deemed unfit as determined by the University Fitness to Practice procedures.
Students who pass the academic but fail the practice component of Placement Two for Professional Practice will be switched to: 08 27169 Reflection on Practice 2.

data.title: LH Practice Education: Stage 1
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

comp: 647B - AdCert Practice Education PT
optional: 7199 - BPhil SpecSocWorkAdults (Flex)

data.restrictions: BPhil Social Work with Children and Young People, their Families and Carers; BPhil Specialist Social Work with Adults, Graduate Affiliate in Social Work with Children and Young People, their Families and Carers; Graduate Affiliate in Specialist Social Work with Adults
description: This module is designed for those supervising, developing and assessing the practice of social work students and other learners. This is both a theoretical and experiential module, which offers participants the opportunity not only to identify and practice the skills of developing, supervising and assessing learners in the workplace, but also to bring an evaluative approach to the impact of education on practice. This applies particularly to supervision and assessment in diverse settings, which promotes equality of opportunity and anti-oppressive practice.

Practice educators who have successfully passed this module will have sufficient experience and have demonstrated competence to directly supervise, teach and assess social work students. They will have demonstrated and provided evidence of how they met the stage 1 Practice Educator Professional Standards (PEPS) and shown a sound value base as a practice educator. Practice educators with this module may contribute to a final placement but will not be able to take full responsibility for assessment or act as the practice educator on a day-to-day basis. They will need stage 2 to be able to take responsibility for this. They will be able to take full responsibility for any other student or be involved in the learning of a final year student.

outcomes.outcome: Critically appraise and organise an effective learning environment for social work learners for the demonstration of assessed competence in practice dealing with complex issues both systematically and creatively commensurate with Stage 1 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain A).

Critically enable the learning and professional development of social work learners in practice by evidencing the ability to teach, facilitate and support their learning and professional development commensurate with Stage 1 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain B).

Demonstrate an ability to critically manage the fair and transparent assessment of social work learners in practice adhering to explicit principles of fairness and equity commensurate with Stage 1 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain C).

Critically evaluate their own continuing development and performance and advance their knowledge and understanding to develop new skills as a practice educator commensurate with Stage 1 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain D).

Demonstrate and evidence the attainment of the practice components, Values Statements, and the 4 Domains (A-D) of BASW's Practice Educator Professional Standards (PEPS) at the level commensurate with Stage 1 Practice Educators.

summative: Academic Assessment: One 4000 word submission (100% of numeric mark)

Practical Assessment: Evidence of supporting a social work learner in practice (as per the PEPS guidance) and a portfolio of work-based evidence and associated commentary to include an observation of the candidates practice (pass/fail).
reassessment: Where students fail their assignment on two separate attempts, they will be automatically awarded with a non-credit bearing, practice only (non-academic) award assuming all professional criteria LO and assessment (see box 19.1 and practical assessment) has been satisfied.

Critically enable the learning and professional development of social work learners in practice by evidencing the ability to teach, facilitate and support their learning and professional development commensurate with Stage 2 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain B).

Critically evaluate their own continuing development and performance and advance their knowledge and understanding to develop new skills as a practice educator commensurate with Stage 2 of the Practice Educator Professional Standards (Domain D).

Demonstrate and evidence the attainment of the practice components, Values Statements, and the 4 Domains (A-D) of BASW's Practice Educator Professional Standards (PEPS) at the level commensurate with Stage 2 Practice Educators.

summative: Academic Assessment: One 2500 word submission (100% of numeric mark)

Practical Assessment: Evidence of supporting a social work learner in practice (as per the PEPS guidance) and a portfolio of work-based evidence and associated commentary to include two observations of the candidates practice (pass/fail).
reassessment: Where students fail their assignment on two separate attempts, they will be automatically awarded with a non-credit bearing, practice only (non-academic) award assuming all professional criteria LO and assessment (see box 19.1 and practical assessment) has been satisfied.

data.title: LH Safeguarding Adults and Social Care Practice with Adults
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

optional: 609A - PGCert Spec Soc Work Adult PT
7199 - BPhil SpecSocWorkAdults (Flex)

data.restrictions: BPhil In Specialist Social Work with Adults, Undergraduate Affiliate in Specialist Social Work with Adults.
description: This module assumes a basic knowledge about the legal, policy and practice framework for safeguarding adults and builds on that foundation by exploring and assessing the impact of ongoing theoretical/conceptual, legal, policy and practice developments and changes in this field of practice for social work practitioners working with vulnerable adults. The module will explore the tensions between intervention and choice, independence and control in responding to potential/actual abuse and prevention.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and describe recent and ongoing legal, policy and practice developments in the field of Safeguarding Adults.
Demonstrate an understanding of how these developments fit into the overall historical emergence of this.
Demonstrate an understanding at both conceptual and practice levels, approaches to understanding and assessing issues of seriousness, vulnerability and risk in relation to safeguarding adults.

Demonstrate an understanding of a range of commonalities and differences within and between perspectives of practitioner, service user and carers perspectives concerning the development and implementation of local Safeguarding Adults procedures and guidelines.
Describe and assess the usefulness of the concept of 'personhood' in the context of Safeguarding Adults practice.
Identify and describe the impact of identity and diversity (e.g. race, ethnicity and culture) on Safeguarding Adults practice.

summative: Oral exam (pass/fail) and a 1500 word critical write up (100% of total mark).

data.title: LH Safeguarding and Care Pathways in Mental Health & Deafness (Advanced)
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: This module examines the complexities of navigating care pathways for D/deaf people with mental health problems to ensure that their social and health care needs are met effectively. The module will include a focus on the need to recognise, respond to and prevent abuse of D/deaf people with mental health problems within the context of care pathways within and across social and health care services.

outcomes.outcome: Evaluate the key Acts of Law and Policy documents relevant to safeguarding D/deaf adults with mental health problems.
Describe the main types of abuse D/deaf people with mental health problems may experience.
Evaluate the causes of vulnerability of D/deaf adults with mental health problems to abuse.
Describe the care pathways available to D/deaf adults with mental health problems.
Evaluate the range of factors that help/hinder D/deaf people with mental health problems navigate care pathways effectively.

data.title: LH Social Perspectives on Mental Health and Deafness (Advanced)
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
description: The module aims to explore relationships between social characteristics and patterns of mental distress; introduce theoretical ideas about both the social construction and social creation of mental illness; and in particular explore how they impact upon the experiences D/deaf people have of mental distress. It will also review the role of social interventions in facilitating the recovery of D/deaf people experiencing mental distress.

outcomes.outcome: Evaluate critically what is meant by the social construction and social creation of mental illness.

Evaluate critically the positive and negative consequences of labelling Evaluate theoretical perspectives that focus on the role of power in the origins of mental distress and the particular role this plays in the mental distress of D/deaf people.
Evaluate social interventions appropriate to work with D/deaf people experiencing mental distress, applying them to their own work experience.

data.title: LH Supervision, Coaching and Mentoring in Organisations
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society

optional: 647B - AdCert Practice Education PT
648B - PGCert Practice Education PT

data.restrictions:
There are no compulsory pre-requisite modules. However:
Completion of at least LH Practice Education Stage 1 Code 08 27335 or LM Practice Education Stage 1 Code 08 27336 or equivalents preferred.
Completion of LH Practice Education Stage 2 Code 08 27315 or LM Practice Education Stage 2 Code 08 27316 preferred or equivalents ideal.
Completion of other post qualifying training plus relevant experience considered.
description: Supervision, Coaching and Mentoring in organisations is a skills focussed module grounded in empirical research, and theoretical knowledge and methodologies from several disciplines. Its starting point is an appreciation that supervision, coaching and mentoring knowledge and skills are fundamental, in combination, to the process of professional development and performance management, and therefore crucial to effective service delivery.

The module aims to prepare students with the knowledge, skills and values required to supervise, coach and mentor social work learners in Social Work, Social Care and Health organisations. It will enable participants to explore and evaluate differing approaches to performance improvement within their role, so reinforcing their leadership/educator role within the organisation.

For those undertaking the module as part of the Advanced or Post Graduate Certificate in Practice Education, the module will connect with and build on the supervision knowledge and skills established within Practice Education Stage1 and Stage 2.

Prospective candidates should note that they are expected to undertake independent study, participate in tutor led activities, connect with their peers to complete practical and reflective activities and organise opportunities for supervisory, coaching and mentoring skills development

outcomes.outcome: Understanding the difference between supervision, coaching and mentoring In reference to research and models for practice
Define the skills and values required for effective supervision, coaching and mentoring conversations and demonstrate these inaction.
Facilitate reflection and negotiate clear learning objectives and action plans  In supervisor, coaching and mentoring encounters
Identify some of the key ethical issues with coaching and mentoring in the workplace.
Self evaluate their effectiveness as a supervisor, coach and or mentor. Their ability to work in anti-oppressive, ethical ways and define future developmental goals.

data.title: LH Transition to Professional Practice
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
coreqs: 08 39611 LH Place Tw fo Professio Pract
description: This module enables students to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the organisational, inter-professional and multi-disciplinary contexts that shape contemporary social practice and how they can effectively thrive as developing practitioners within them. It provides students with a critical awareness of the importance of self-management and professional identity, so they are better equipped to understand the nature, and thus be able to evaluate theoretical approaches to effectively managing organisational change and conflict.

As you prepare for entry to qualified social worker status you will be able to demonstrate a critical understanding of theories of emotional intelligence and emotional resilience and their application to practice and to effective professional relationships and a critical awareness of different structural and organisational power relationships and how to construct appropriate responses to thrive in practice.

outcomes.outcome: Critique the role and nature of professional identity within the workplace and how it can be promoted within inter-professional and multi-disciplinary contexts.
Develop awareness and skills in self-management and emotional intelligence.
Devise strategies to work proactively within social work organisational contexts demonstrating value-based leadership skills.
Specify and critically assess the manifestations of organisational power and how to affect positive change within organisational settings.

reassessment: Re-assessment by failed component where a student has failed to pass the module at the first attempt.

Describe and evaluate the impact of different models of disability and vulnerability on the organisation and delivery of community and residential services to adults.
Describe and evaluate different strategies for working with and where possible avoiding the development of conflict between different disciplines and agencies within adult care services.

data.title: LI Critical Social Work Practice with Children, Families and Adults
data.school: School of Soc Pol and Society
