Although, for each student, individual experiences in this required component may be measured in days rather than weeks, the overall commitment of our placement partners over the whole year and across cohorts is substantial and every care will be taken to ensure the quality and safety of learning experiences and compliance with the Code of Practice for placement learning.

For each placement, detailed information about learning tasks will be provided to students and their supervisors, along with clear guidance with regard to what they can and cannot expect of each other. From the perspective of the placement, this will largely be about supervision and feedback rather than teaching, but any required training (e.g. on the use of equipment in practice) will be specified. Supervisors will be involved in assessing student performance (and their reflection on performance) as satisfactory / unsatisfactory, but the overall assessment of the component is managed by the programme team. In hospital settings, students will be supervised by teacher / practitioner academics. In other settings, academics from the programme team will take a more active role in supporting supervisors.

outcomes.outcome: By the end of the component students should be able to:
Reflect how guidance produced by the General Pharmaceutical Council is applied and interpreted in day to day professional practice with reference to pharmacy placement experience.
Recognise and describe ethical issues related to pharmacy practice, interprofessional working and patient care, which have arisen during professional experience placements.
Describe the role of team working and communication in improving patient safety with reference to placement experiences.
Demonstrate a reflective approach to communication opportunities with patients, health care professionals, and `workplace? colleagues.

summative: Demonstration of professional attitudes, teamwork and communication with patients and professional colleagues through direct observation and through learning tasks submitted via ePortfolio assessed by placement practitioners.ePortfolio submission at the end of the year assessed by academic staff.

data.title: Research Methods
description: This module provides students with the knowledge and skills required to support and underpin the research project module.

Delivered through a series of face to face lectures, supported by online material and small group tutorials, students will develop an understanding of qualitative and quantitative research methodologies and associated methods of data analysis.

Students will be assessed by their ability to formulate research questions which are open to exploration through a range of paradigms and choose appropriate methods to address them. data.title: Science of Medicines 1
description: This module will provide students with an understanding of a range of routes of administration of pharmaceutical dosage forms, and an appreciation of the formulation principles and manufacturing methods used in the preparation of liquid and semi-solid dosage forms.  The module will also address pre-formulation studies and the concept of bioavailability.

Material will be taught using a combination of large group lectures and small group workshops, along with the provision of online material.  The theoretical elements of the module will be supported through practical laboratory experiments and a pharmaceutical problem solving exercise.
Assessment will be through written examinations (MCQ, SAQ), written practical laboratory experiment write-ups and completion of the pharmaceutical problem solving exercise.

All modules are integrative. Students will develop an appreciation of how knowledge gained through this module may be applied to other first year modules, specifically The Professional Pharmacist, Health, Disease and Therapeutics 1 and 2 and Chemistry for Pharmacists 1. This application of knowledge will be further tested throughout the course progression.

outcomes.outcome: Apply prior learning to and integrate it with the new learning content of this module;
Discuss how the choice of dosage form and route of administration of a medicine are influenced by the intended therapeutic outcome, site of action and physicochemical properties of the drug;
Extemporaneously prepare a range of liquid and semi-solid pharmaceutical dosage forms;

Describe and discuss the properties and formulation of liquid (solutions, suspensions, emulsions) and semi-solid (creams, ointments, pastes, gels, suppositories, pessaries) dosage forms, with reference to pharmaceutically-important examples;
Describe the necessity for pre-formulation studies and discuss the relationship between physicochemical properties of a drug and potential formulation difficulties;
Discuss how the bioavailability of a drug is influenced by its physicochemical properties, the dosage form and the route of administration.

data.title: The Professional Pharmacist 1
description: Delivered throughout the first year, this module applies and integrates all of the year 1 modules with the professional practice of pharmacy and in addition delivers material forming the basis of more advanced study, which may be applied and tested in later modules.

The treatment of minor ailments (self diagnosed) linked to other first year modules will be covered, aiming to equip the student with the basic skills in communication and related therapeutic knowledge required to discuss over the counter remedies with patients. This will act as the first step towards history taking, shared decision-making and applied therapeutic decision-making.

This module introduces the students to the legal and ethical environment, which pharmacists work within. The relevant UK and EU law, and its application to the supply and dispensing of medicines, will be taught (Including knowledge of classification of medicines). Students will be introduced to ethical frameworks and their application to professional scenarios.

Key concepts in Evidence Based Medicine will be introduced, as well as information mastery skills that will form the basis for finding trusted sources of appropriate information to inform clinical decision-making.

This module will introduce the students to the pharmacy role in public health. Students will also be taught the structure and organisation of healthcare systems, with particular reference to the NHS and associated bodies.

Mathematical skills will be taught, and related to other first year modules, and put in the context of safe pharmaceutical practice. Students will also be introduced to key concepts in human factors, including human error theory, in relation to the potential for human error in healthcare systems. This will be used and integrated into all clinical communication work.

Through a series of lectures, workshops (including simulated patients), small group teaching supported with online reference material, and professional experience `placements? students will become comfortable with basic consultation skills and conducting a cranial nerve examination.

Assessment will reflect the applied and professional nature of this module using objective structured clinical examination (OSCEs) to demonstrate capability in communication, clinical and dispensing skills.
Public health, Evidence based medicine, human factors, and healthcare systems will be examined using MCQs and SAQs.
Separate examinations will be held in Law and Ethics, and in Mathematics. These are must pass elements of the module.
Coursework will include an Evidence Based Medicine assignment, and a Pharmacy and Public Health campaign.

outcomes.outcome: Apply prior learning to and integrate it with the new learning content of this module.
Describe the different models underpinning our understanding of illness behaviour and how this might affect attitudes towards medicines.

Demonstrate competence in agreed elements of modern dispensing, record keeping, and the application of relevant legislation.

Explain key concepts in Evidence Based Medicine and information mastery and their application to clinical questions.
Demonstrate competence in pharmaceutical calculations and numeracy.
Demonstrate an understanding of healthcare systems in the United Kingdom, with specific reference to the NHS, and the contribution of pharmacy.
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant legislation pertaining to Equality and Diversity, and Safeguarding.
Explain basic concepts in human factors in relation to the potential for human error in healthcare systems.

data.title: The Professional Pharmacist 3
description: Delivered throughout the third year, this module applies and integrates learning from all of the year 3 modules with the professional practice of pharmacy and in addition delivers material forming the basis of more advanced study, which may be applied and tested in later modules.  This module places such material into a patient context and within the legal frameworks governing the supply of medicines. A strong emphasis will be placed on the development of communication skills and patient management.

This module will further develop student knowledge and skills in evidence-based medicine, and its application to clinical practice. More detailed information on the design and management of clinical trials and post-marketing studies will be provided, along with their application to the assessment of efficacy, effectiveness, and safety. Principles of Health economics will also be taught. The common complementary alternative medicines systems will be taught within a framework of evidence-based medicine.

Further knowledge on the harm from medicines, error theory, and methods of preventing or mitigating such harms will be taught, and students will apply this knowledge to solve problem scenarios. Students will be introduced to the concept of clinical governance.
Students will also be taught basic principles of the use of drugs within veterinary practice with an emphasis on companion animals.

The teaching of law will continue, with examination of regulations concerning veterinary practice, complementary and alternative medicines, poisons, and drugs of abuse. Additional material on the professional regulation of pharmacy will be taught, alongside its relationship to other professional organisations within pharmacy and other professions. Students should expect to deal with more complex ethical considerations.

Assessment will reflect the applied and professional nature of this module using objective structured clinical examination (OSCEs) to demonstrate capability in communication, clinical and dispensing skills.
Written examinations will focus on the application of knowledge using a variety of applied written tasks, some details of which will be specified prior to the examination.
Coursework will include the critical appraisal of a scientific paper, set out as a presentation to a hospital or primary care organisation, and a written report analysing a medical error.

Demonstrate application and communication of pharmaceutical knowledge, including in specialised patient groups and in challenging situations, including within an interprofessional context.
Demonstrate an understanding of advanced evidence based medicine, including evaluation and communication of benefit and harms.
Demonstrate an understanding of clinical trials and post-marketing study design and management.
Critically appraise a scientific paper.
Demonstrate an understanding of health economics, including key concepts such as value for money, efficiency, opportunity cost, and their applicability to evidence based decision making.
Demonstrate understanding of the regulation and evidence-base of herbal, homeopathic, and other complementary medicines.
Demonstrate continuing competence in modern dispensing, record keeping, and the application of relevant legislation.
Demonstrate an understanding of veterinary law and the use of drugs in veterinary practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of the regulation of the profession of pharmacy, and its relationship to other professional bodies within pharmacy and other professions.
Demonstrate an understanding of the law relating to the misuse of drugs, the use of drugs of abuse by society, and the treatment of addiction.
Demonstrate an understanding of the law related to the supply of poisons and pesticides in the UK.
Justify decisions in complex ethical and professional problems in healthcare.
Demonstrate competence in pharmaceutical calculations and numeracy.

description: This module covers the underlying principles of adult learning and their applicability to use in multidisciplinary healthcare simulation. Teaching for this module takes place over a period of 5 days and is provided in two blocks; an initial block of teaching over a period of 3 days, followed by a block of teaching over 2 days. A 4 week break between blocks of teaching has been scheduled to allow students time for reflection and preparation for the assessed oral presentations on day 5 of the module.

The module will be offered to students as either CPD or as an accredited module. The students undertaking the accreditation will be registered with the UoB. To be awarded module credits, students undertaking the accredited module will be required to successfully complete an oral presentation and evidence based written assignment.

Academics within the School of Health and Population Sciences at the UoB will provide academic oversight and teaching support to include quality assurance of course content and second marking of assignments. As such, this module is owned by UoB.

outcomes.outcome: Understand the relevant educational principles of adult learning and how these concepts are used in multidisciplinary healthcare simulation. (Assessed through essay);

Understand the principles of experiential learning and how this is directly applicable to learning using multidisciplinary healthcare simulation techniques. (Assessed through essay).

description: The module aims to provide a reproducible educational framework for clinicians involved in anticoagulation management.

The course will produce a critical awareness of new insights into the area of anticoagulation management and provide advanced knowledge and skills to enable autonomous practice in dealing with more complex problems.
The module will comprise:
1. Pre-course reading material containing self-assessment material at the conclusion of each chapter.

This will provide the theoretical background to the subject and help the student to provide a critical appreciation of areas discussed within the taught course. Students will be asked to provide evidence of current literature review when responding to the self assessment exercises.
2. Three days contact time involving:
Lectures from specialists in the field who will discuss the key theoretical and clinical aspects of anticoagulation management.
Group work where students will contribute to discussion, analysis and application of the theoretical perspectives that underpin practice.
Practical workshops provide practical experience for the students, an opportunity to develop protocols and to reflect on requirements for auditing the process.
A theory exam, 35 item MCQ paper

Practical assessment will be undertaken using clinical scenarios centred on anticoagulation management. The students will be expected to demonstrate a clear understanding of the clinical issues,  participate in decision making and problem solving practice which will include examples of tackling and solving complex problems
3.Written evidence based protocol.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a systematic, conceptual understanding of the theory underpinning anticoagulation management (MCQ exam and pre course work self assessment exercises).
Demonstrate an ability to apply concepts appropriately in dealing with novel and complex clinical situations (MCQ exam and practical assessment).
Understand the pharmacology of vitamin K antagonists and determine the relevant medication, side effects, antidotes, interactions and dosing. (Protocol).
Understand the management of anticoagulation and prevention of complications on the basis of current guidelines and existing research evidence. (Protocol).

Demonstrate an understanding of the roles of the multi professional disciplinary team in managing anticoagulation safely and the importance of i) multi-disciplinary teamwork in improving health outcomes, and ii) when referral is appropriate. (Written evidence based protocol).

summative: Clinical protocol (70%) - Should this component be failed, the existing protocol should be modified and re-submitted.
Students will be expected to pass all elements of the summative assessment to receive an overall pass.
reassessment: Students not obtaining a pass on any of the assessments will be required to re sit the failed element and the mark will be set at 50%

data.title: Effects of Work on Health and Fitness for Work
description: The first part of this module covers the adverse impact that harmful exposures and practices at work may have on health, the skills of diagnosis and attribution of ill health to work and the application of evidence-based decisions to prevent ill health. Topics include a systems exploration of disease and injury (focusing largely on classical occupational diseases and cross-linked to other modules on the MSc OH course) health screening and surveillance.

The second half of the module examines the impact health and fitness may have on the capability of an individual for useful work and how evidence-based decisions may be made to strike the proper balance between safety and minimising restrictions on employability. Topics will include: setting task-related health and fitness standards for employment: adapting work to minimise health and fitness restrictions; applying task-related standards to pre-employment, during employment and when determining if and when employment should be terminated.  Reference is made to a range of occupational cases and their diagnosis in presentations. The use bio-medical equipment for health screening is demonstrated including interpretation of data.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate understanding of and competence within their professional sphere for assessing the impact of work activities on health.
Advise on the Clinical diagnosis of occupational disease.
Critically review work related hazards and risks and set appropriate standards of protection of the health and fitness of workers in a range of occupations.
Provide advice on appropriate health screening and health surveillance.

Play a lead part as an occupational health manager and a specialist in their professional discipline in advising management on setting task-related standards of health and fitness for a range of occupations and workplace adjustments.
Adapt work to maximise an individual's ability and minimise the effects of ill health or reduced fitness.
Determine how work may be adapted to achieve the  balance between safety and minimising restrictions on employability.

summative: Essay (2500-3000 words): with two components assessing (a) effect of work on health (b) fitness for work

description: This module utilises the learning in earlier modules from years 1 to 3, in particular, evidence based medicine and research methods which is undertaken in the first semester of year 3. Working in self-selected groups of between four and five, students will identify their own clinical case, scenario, health services issue or population based health problem to base their evidence review upon. This could be from year 3 clinical experience in hospital or primary care, or a topic area that students have an established specialist interest in (e.g. public health, health service delivery & organisation). Groups will utilise the four As to conduct a detailed evidence review in the form of a 4000 word report in relation to their chosen scenario: Assess - articulate a clear question for the review based on the scenario chosen; Access - construct and conduct relevant literature searches in order to identify relevant evidence, clinical summaries and guidelines; Appraise - critically appraise and review the results of those literature reviews; Act - interpret the evidence in relation to clinical practice and policy; identify areas for future research. Groups will be allocated an advisor (staff within the Institute of Applied Health Research) by the module leads. Advisors will assist with the formulation of review ideas, provide formative support on the linked outline and progress review activity, and one set of detailed comments on a final draft of the evidence review.  Groups will submit one report with each student within that group being allocated the same mark. To try to ensure equality of workload, students will be asked as part of their outline plan to provide brief information on what each student will contribute to the project. This will be revisited as part of the progress review activity and formative discussion with their advisor. In addition, students will be asked to submit a contribution statement with their project which will be reviewed by the marker.

outcomes.outcome: Identify and describe a clinical case, scenario, health service issue or population-based health problem that is of interest to you and your group peers
Define and articulate a review question related to this case, scenario, issue or problem (Assess)
Use and demonstrate a systematic approach to literature searching to identify evidence relevant to the review question including guidelines, systematic reviews, and primary studies (Access)
Critically appraise and evaluate the literature using appropriate tools and checklists  (Appraise)
Critically interpret and articulate the implications of the evidence review in relation to individual clinician and health service policy and practice (Act)
Write a concise, clearly articulated and critical evidence review
Demonstrate the ability to build positive peer relationships and undertake required team roles to successfully design, deliver and write the evidence review

summative: Linked outline plan and progress review: 5%
reassessment: Re-submission of full evidence review which will contribute 100% of the resubmission mark

description: To provide accredited certification and validation of competencies for health care professionals involved in the management of people with heart failure in the community.

The course has been produced to offer a systematic understanding of heart failure and a knowledge of how to apply this knowledge to practice; a critical awareness of current management issues and new insights into the management of heart failure.

It will also provide skills to enable autonomous practice in dealing with more complex problems and unpredictable situations and the ability to critically evaluate current research in the heart failure arena.  An independent learning process will allow students to continue to advance their knowledge and understanding of heart failure.
The course is in line with the approaches set out in the NICE guidelines for Heart Failure and the Quality and Outcome Framework indicators for good practice.

4) Demonstrate an understanding of the requirements of clinical governance for heart failure management, developing audit tools and performance indicators to ensure local services are being delivered to an acceptable standard of care.

data.title: LC Health Protection
description: Health protection describes the range of public health activities that aim to prevent and control infectious diseases and other environmental threats to the health of the population. It is central to the work public health practitioners. The module will provide an introduction to key concepts in health protection and will allow students to develop an understanding of the principles of health protection and specific interventions, including partnership working to deliver health protection services in a variety of national and international settings.

The module will consider the structures and services required to deliver effective local, national and international health protection arrangements; emergency planning, risk assessment and communication; the principles of surveillance; the principles of incident/outbreak investigation and control; and introduce key environmental, communicable disease and radiological hazards, as well the main interventions available to control these.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the major health protection risks that inform the practice of public health.
Understand the principles of investigating and controlling communicable diseases and non-communicable environmental hazards, and be able to justify solutions to common problems
Understand the principles of disease and hazard surveillance, and describe local, national and international surveillance systems.

Analyse and interpret information obtained following an investigation of a communicable disease outbreak and/or non-communicable public health hazard, including the principles of investigating disease clusters.
Appreciate the specific contributions of various agencies and organisations to health protection and the basic principles of emergency planning and response.

data.title: LC Individual, Cultural and Societal Determinants of Health
description: This module introduces the students to the social determinants of health.  Its focus will be on those factors that are typically termed `lifestyle?; that is, on (a) diet and physical activity; (b) the use of smoking, alcohol and drugs; and (c) sexual behaviour and activity.  These so-called `lifestyle choices? will be studied in the social context in which they occur and their impacts will be examined across the lifecourse and in relation to health inequalities. While this module will introduce students to the complete range of determinants of health, non-lifestyle determinants will be picked up in detail in other modules (e.g. parenting and early psychological development (in Mental Health); homelessness (Built and Natural Environments); employment (Economics and Politics of Public Health))

In the first part of the module students will be introduced to frameworks used to conceptualise the determinants of health and health inequalities; theories of health behaviour, choice and behaviour change; critical race and gender theory, including intersectionality; and concepts of social cohesion and capital.  The module's focus will then move to consider the key `lifestyle behaviours?.  Week 11 will wrap up the module, using the WHO Global Commission on Social Determinants of Health as a basis to review and integrate learning.

outcomes.outcome: Describe key theories and models of the determinants of health
Describe key theories and models of health behaviour (focusing specifically on `lifestyle? choices and behaviours) and behavioural change.
Describe the epidemiology, health and societal effects of key health behaviours.
Explain the relationship between health behaviours and health inequalities.
Describe how social and community factors impact on health and health behaviours

summative: The pass mark for the module is 40%

description: This module introduces students to public health and global health. The module is designed to give the students a good understanding of public health at a local, national and global scale and the associated challenges and opportunities. The range of topics covered include: how public health is organised, who practices it, and the key skills underpinning the discipline. Global health features prominently to give the students a broader understanding of public health in an international context. Global health is an area for study, research, and practice that places a priority on improving health and achieving equity in health for all people worldwide. Global health emphasizes transnational health issues, determinants, and solutions; involves many disciplines within and beyond the health sciences and promotes interdisciplinary collaboration; and is a synthesis of population-based prevention with individual-level clinical care. The history of public health in the UK enables the students to develop a broader understanding of how the discipline has evolved, its impact and its relevance to wider society. The mechanisms contributing to health inequalities and the wider determinants of health are key threads that the students will carry with them through the rest of the course. How the 16 modules of the BSc Public Health programme fit together and a brief introduction to these modules will also be covered.

outcomes.outcome: Describe public health and global health in terms of key concepts, domains, activities and skills.
Discuss the history of public health and global health in relation to individuals, institutions and society, demonstrating insight into how history is constructed.
Describe the structure of the health systems, social care and public health both nationally and globally
Discuss evidence for the presence of health inequalities both nationally and globally
Discuss the wider determinants of health and their relationship to inequalities in health, and how this varies across the life course.
Compare key public health issues within a range of national and global contexts

summative: 1500 word essay (50%) and an unseen examination consisting of short-answer questions (50%)
The pass mark for the module is 40%

data.title: LC Physical and Mental Health
description: This module ensures the student has the basic understanding necessary for dealing with the key public health issues of our times. Students will be introduced to physical and mental health and wellbeing, including non-communicable and communicable diseases of public health importance. Students will learn about the epidemiology, risk factors and preventive (primary, secondary and tertiary) strategies for these diseases. Students will examine these diseases in relation to health inequalities. Students will also consider how and why disease profiles differ globally.

Mental health is vital to population health as mental wellbeing profoundly influences our quality of life and our resilience to inevitable changes in circumstance. The ways in which mental wellbeing can protect individuals against physical illness, inequities and unhealthy behaviour will be explored.

data.title: LC The Built and Natural Environment
description: Research clearly demonstrates that the built and natural environment has a significant impact on the physical and mental health and wellbeing of the population. There are clear inequities in both the exposure to environmental hazards and access to environmental assets such as green space predicated by deprivation.  In addition, there is emerging evidence that deprivation modifies susceptibility to the effects of those exposures.

A century ago planning, engineering and public health professionals worked together to ensure development reduced the spread of disease. These professions diverged as public health followed a more clinical model but they are now re-converging to once again ensure the linkages between the built and natural environment and public health inform the development of our towns and cities.

This module describes how factors such as the house we live in, the air we breathe, how we travel, the green space we access, the soil in our gardens, and the energy from the sun all impact on our physical and mental health and wellbeing. We examine the drivers (such as globalisation, the planning system, economic development) that produce the areas we live in. We will examine how to maximise the health gains from positive impacts such as green space and how to minimise the health risks from harmful factors such as the obesogenic environment.

We will also explore how public health works with other professions, especially urban planning and transportation. This will examine the interface between disciplines who have different understandings of what constitutes evidence and how this can be applied to real world practice globally.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the relationship between the built and natural environment and public health
Describe how the built and natural environment can influence health inequities and impact on vulnerable populations
Describe interventions that maximise the public health benefit of good quality built and natural environments.
Understand the process of undertaking a Health Impact Assessment
Gain an understanding of how different professions use evidence and how public health must work with other disciplines to improve population health

data.title: Legal Aspects
description: The module aims to give students a systematic understanding of how the legal process has influenced and continues to influence the development of occupational health both nationally and internationally. Factors contributing to the shaping of legal aspects of occupational health practice are also discussed.

The module brings together from all other modules the role of the regulatory process within occupational health.  The participants in this module will gain a comprehensive understanding of relevant legislation within the UK and EU framework.

The module includes: Review of how law making, regulatory and legal processes have influenced the evolution of occupational health practice and their current relevance for the practitioner; State involvement in Occupational Health and Safety including Health and Safety risks and the English legal system; Development and implementation of risk management systems, the role of the HSE and local authority inspectors; Employment law including discrimination, DDA and performance at work.
The students will learn on how legislation relevant to occupational health is applied and interpreted including the implications for non-compliance.

Critically evaluate the legal implications for an organisation conducting various activities with health, safety and environmental implications.

data.title: LH Dissertation
prereqs: 01 30524 LC Intro to Pub Health Researc
description: The dissertation enables the student to demonstrate the application of their knowledge and skills in the fields of public health and epidemiology. It is designed to test the student's ability to plan, carry out and report a research study addressing a question that is relevant to public health. The students will have gained the necessary skills in the three public health research modules in Years 1, 2 and 3 (Introduction to Public Health Research, Public Health Research Skills, Public Health Research in Practice). This module will test their creative, planning, analytical, evaluative, writing, presentation and organisational skills.

Students will need to: (1) with support, identify an area of interest; (2) explore an area in depth; (3) define their own question; (4) obtain the necessary research ethical approval for the proposed project; (5) manage a project from beginning to end; and (6) consolidate their communication, information-seeking and intellectual skills.

Define a research question relevant to a current public health problem

Determine appropriate methods of investigation, justifying the approach and tools selected and recognising their limitations
Collect, record, analyse and interpret or review and critically analyse relevant data or information.

Discuss their findings in the context of current scientific knowledge, discuss the significance of their findings for public health and develop an action plan or recommendations arising from the project.
Present results and ideas in an appropriate written format.

description: This module aims to equip students with skills needed to conceive, design and conduct a feasible piece of research in the field of global health suitable for publication within a relevant journal. Students will experience data collection, management and analysis, prior to writing up in the form of an academic paper or dissertation.

Project supervisors will be allocated in consultation with the module co-ordinator.  Students will meet with their supervisor(s) in Semester 1 to develop a research proposal for the project to be carried out in Semester 2, with further supervisory meetings throughout.    If necessary, ethical approval for the proposed project will be obtained and scoping work (e.g. familiarisation with local policy and practice) undertaken.  The module is delivered across the first and second semesters.

There will be group contact time and teaching in the first semester will involve lectures and seminars where students will meet to discuss project ideas and development. Towards the end of Semester 1, each student will give an oral presentation (summative assessment - 10% of module) of the research proposal to the group, submitting a written research proposal for formative assessment.  They will also make submissions to the Internal Research Ethics Committee as appropriate for their chosen project.  In Semester 2 students will work under close supervision to conduct their research project.  Students will have tutorials with their supervisor on a regular basis and these will identify problems with data collection, monitor progress and support data management and delivery, enabling the student to fully engage with the research process from concept to completion.

Students will also have access to statistics and research skills clinics throughout both semesters to supplement supervision.Towards the end of Semester 2 students will present an academic poster of their research findings (summative assessment ? 15% of module) and will also submit their project write up either as a dissertation or academic paper written in the style of an appropriate journal (summative assessment ? 75% of module).

description: This module will give a comprehensive introduction to medical statistics and show why it is an important application of mathematical and statistical theory. The module will use statistical methods learnt in other modules, and also introduce some new statistical concepts and methods, with application to real medical problems and healthcare research. The module is split into 5 sections. In Epidemiology, students will cover the analysis of diagnostic test studies; the design and analysis of cohort studies and case-control studies; the use and interpretation of linear and logistic regression models; and the problem of confounding factors. In Survival Analysis students will consider how to analyse censored time-to-event data; the specification and interpretation of hazard and survival functions; the estimation of Kaplan-Meier curves; and the use and interpretation of Cox regression models. In Clinical Trials students will consider the rationale and design of randomised controlled trials; the derivation and application of sample size equations; and the analysis of parallel group trials and cross-over trials. In Systematic Reviews students will consider how to synthesise multiple studies and produce evidence-based results; show the differences between fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analysis models; show how to measure, account for, and explain between-study heterogeneity; and appreciate how to assess publication bias. Finally, in Bayesian Statistics students will cover the differences between Bayesian and frequentist statistical inference; work through the Bayesian analysis of a clinical trial; derive and interpret posterior probability distributions; and utilise the computer software FirstBayes.

outcomes.outcome: Appreciate how medical statistics plays a fundamental role in understanding health and diseases in the population;
Understand why medical statistics informs clinical practice and the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of patients;
Understand the rationale for and design of cohort studies, case-control studies, clinical trials, and systematic reviews;
Understand, apply and interpret a range of statistical methods in the context of epidemiological studies, diagnostic tests, clinical trials, survival analysis, and systematic reviews;
Apply mathematical theory to derive unbiased estimates of disease risk in different groups of patients, and to interpret their uncertainty by calculating confidence intervals and p-values;
Understand and interpret regression models for continuous, binary and survival data;
Understand the differences between Bayesian and classical statistical inference, and perform Bayesian statistical analyses of medical data.

data.title: LI Global Health
description: This module places the health of populations in a global context, and enables a greater awareness of global health related issues. It will broaden a range of principles and topics learnt in other modules with a focus on health for all people worldwide. Themes studied in previous modules will be put in the context of resource poor settings with examples in a range of continents and low and middle income countries (LMICs).

This is a broad module that covers communicable diseases such as Ebola and HIV/AIDS, non-communicable disease (NCDs) such as cardiovascular diseases and maternal and child health, that are an increasing burden in LMICs, global issues such as climate change, war/natural disaster, and healthcare

There is a strong theme of social justice and equity that runs through the course. This will be linked to prominent global development and health agendas such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The module examines the role of government and non-government organisations, global agencies, private providers and communities of all capacity to alleviate the health problems that countries face.

A significant component of the module is the development of ideas into a project plan /proposal for an intervention project for a vulnerable group in a LMIC. This group exercise with its own learning objectives will also form the basis for the assessment.

data.title: LI Healthcare Public Health
description: Healthcare public health is one of the three core domains of specialist public health practice. It is concerned with maximising the population benefits of healthcare while meeting the needs of individuals and groups through prioritising available resources, preventing disease, and by improving health-related outcomes through design, access, utilisation and evaluation of effective and efficient healthcare interventions and pathways of care.

The module will introduce students to the commissioning cycle and the three key areas of planning, procuring and monitoring health care services. The module is underpinned by teaching on the critical appraisal of evidence and the use of economic appraisal in health settings. Particular emphasis is placed on health needs assessment, health technology assessment, priority setting, service design/re-design, commissioning, quality improvement and assurance, and the evaluation of health services.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the commissioning cycle in the context of health care and public health service commissioning.
Understand of the principles and practice of health care needs assessment and its application in public health practice.
Analyse the implementation of health care policy, in particular through the prioritisation of services and interventions at local and national levels.
Describe critical steps in health service (re)design, such as service specification, and understand the care pathway and models of care.

Discuss the need for health technology assessment and understand the information and evidence requirements for healthcare policy making in the context of new and existing health interventions and technologies.
Understand the principles of evaluation and audit in the context of assuring and improving the quality of health care.

data.title: LI Health Improvement
description: Health improvement is defined as the process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants, and thereby improve their health. It is central to the work of public health practitioners. This module will enable students to critically analyse health improvement policy, research, methods and strategies at a regional, national and international scale.

The module will consider the scope of health improvement and promotion; health promotion theories, models and strategies; changing behaviour; patient and public participation in health improvement; collaboration, partnerships, joint working and community development; ethics, ideology, power and politics relevant to health improvement; and the commissioning, planning and evaluation of health improvement and health promotion.

sameLevelModule.title: LI Health Improvement
description: Health improvement is defined as the process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants, and thereby improve their health. It is central to the work of public health practitioners. This module will enable students to critically analyse health improvement policy, research, methods and strategies at a regional, national and international scale.

The module will consider the scope of health improvement and promotion; health promotion theories, models and strategies; changing behaviour; patient and public participation in health improvement; collaboration, partnerships, joint working and community development; ethics, ideology, power and politics relevant to health improvement; and the commissioning, planning and evaluation of health improvement and health promotion.

outcomes.outcome: Understand the breadth of health improvement activity and describe this in terms of individuals, groups, communities and regions/countries.
Understand and be able to discuss key theories and research that underpin evidence based approaches to health improvement.
Propose health improvement priorities at all levels (local, regional, national and international), and be able to critically discuss strategies and methods to address these.
Understand the principles of evaluating health improvement strategies, policies and activities, and demonstrate how to apply these in practice.
Understand how issues of power, ethics and politics influence health improvement strategies, policy and practice.

summative: Individual written assignment - 3,000 word proposal for or critical analysis of a health improvement problem or strategy
The pass mark for the module is 40%
reassessment: One opportunity to resubmit the written assignment.

data.title: LI Public Health Ethics and Law
description: Of the greatest public health achievements of the twentieth century, all had some basis in legislation and regulation: vaccinations; safer workplaces; safer and healthier foods; motor vehicle safety; control of infectious diseases; the decline in deaths from coronary heart disease and stroke; family planning; tobacco control; healthier mothers and babies; and fluoridation of drinking water. Public health law will continue to play an important part in the health of the population (for example in the fields of air quality and climate change). It is therefore critical for students to understand how the law can be used to improve population health and understand the legal processes involved in influencing the relationships between individuals, the public and the state.

The duty to protect and improve public health, must also be weighed against an individual's rights, for example to liberty, privacy and freedom of association. An understanding of ethical frameworks is required to help public health professionals balance these competing values, and develop ethically defensible decisions making.

This module provides students with a grounding in ethics and law in the context of public health. The first half of the module introduces key concepts and theories. The second half focuses on specific public health case studies, allowing the application of knowledge and skills.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of ethics and law in the context of public health
Demonstrate an awareness of the competing/conflicting interests between people, communities, and the state.
Demonstrate skills in analysis and argument developed through discussion of relevant case studies
Describe the impact of law and regulation on the health of the public

summative: 20% group presentation on one of the case studies.
The pass mark for the module is 40%
reassessment: One resubmission of the written assignment. For group presentation, students will have one opportunity to present individually.

data.title: LM Alternative Payment Models
prereqs: 07 26552 LM Intro to Lead Manage Health
description: Economic thinking plays an important role in population health management at all levels. Patients, providers, and payers involved in the health care sector make decisions that are partly based on economic incentives, which are often manipulated to achieve the overarching system goals. Knowledge of the underlying logic and employed terminology of payment reforms, are useful to influence health policy and increase value of health care services.

This course is intended to teach students how to analyse current population health management issues through the application of basic economic principles. No previous economics training is required. The course will begin with an introduction to health economics. Among the topics we will discuss are health insurance coverage, provider payer incentives and competition. Subsequently, the basic concepts, key designs elements, implementation strategies and evaluation method of payment reforms will be introduced. Topics that will be discussed include base payment models (e.g. fee-for-services, capitation) and alternative payment models (e.g. pay-for-performance, shared savings, bundled payment, global payments). As payment reforms aim to change provider behaviour, we will also focus on the role of behavioural economics.

outcomes.outcome: Can recognize health economic issues as they arise in health care practice and health policy around the world.
Can critique and form economic arguments for and against particular health policies and argue the rationale for the need for alternative payment models.
Can describe key health economic concepts including efficiency, asymmetric information, agency, moral hazard, and adverse election.
Can describe key concepts regarding alternative payment models including shared savings and bundled payment
Can apply insights from behavioural economic theories within the design of alternative payment models of behavioural economics including loss aversion.
Can reflect on the different base- and add-on payment models, their incentives and potential consequences for provider behaviour.

summative: Final creative assignment (50%) includes a written plan of action (600-800 words), creative form of the assignment e.g. short video/infographic/podcast, and cover letter (1200-1500 words) that is due at the end of the four weeks that the module runs.
reassessment: If the overall mark is less than 55% or if the student did not complete all three components of assessment, then the student is given the opportunity to re-sit the assessment as one assignment that covers all the learning goals of the course.

data.title: LM Building Foundations for Primary Care Team Effectiveness
description: This module focuses on teams in primary care. It begins by working with students to develop a clear understanding of the team they lead: the team's purpose, its members and the community or ethos of the team. It then develops an understanding of the foundations required for effective team working in primary care. This includes aligning individuals? practice with the primary care team's shared values. It also includes creating a team climate which values differences between members (e.g. different clinical perspectives) and makes use of these differences. The module works through a series of steps that enable team leaders to establish a culture which makes others feel safe to discuss concerns, make suggestions and provide constructive debate. This will include, examining team member engagement and team dynamics, understanding how diversity influences team effectiveness, team conflict resolution, developing team positivity, exploring inter-team working and contextual constraints.

Demonstrate knowledge of how leadership practice improves and sustains care quality.
Demonstrate practical skills to embed diversity, equality and inclusion in leadership practices

description: This module is designed to go beyond the first principles of economic evaluation. Its focus will be the development, extension and application of the main issues and techniques fro economic evaluation that were discussed in the introductory module. The material covered by the course includes an in depth coverage of the components of economics evaluations, such as, cost data collection and analysis, outcome data analysis, health state valuation in general and discounting issues. Alternative methods for economic evaluation and the relevant frameworks will be discussed with case studies and policy applications. The module includes a full day's inter-active practical session in which 'hands-on' application and analysis of alternative modelling approaches used in economic evaluation will be demonstrated with full discussion of the advantages and appropriateness of the alternative techniques.

Critically review alternative methods to outcome evaluation and their relevance to alternative evaluation approaches
Recognise the policy implications that may result from economic evaluations.

description: This module is to be introduced as part of the proposed new MSc in Genomic Medicine.

With the UK government's effort to develop national clinical guidelines to secure consistent, high quality, evidence-based medicine predicated on outcomes and cost, it is important that students understand the role of economic modelling in the decision-making process. The module will explore the potential impact of genomic technologies on the healthcare system. Economic models will be used to demonstrate the anticipated costs and benefits of new technological approaches.

Technological advances in the area of genomic medicine have led to new tests with major impact on improving disease diagnosis and effectiveness of treatments. However, the continuous growth in the use of genomic technologies has cost implications. Using established economic models it is possible to predict the costs of new treatments and assess benefits to patients in the context of the available resources for health care. In addition, this module will explore the factors that determine the effects of the rapid development of genomics on health care systems covering the role and relative influence that government, doctors and the public exert in this process. These will be analysed to assess whether clients/patients are best served by current arrangements and whether people's health outcomes match reasonable expectations. Students will be encouraged to propose ways of tackling perceived shortcomings.

outcomes.outcome: Appreciate the role of `quality of life? studies in outcome evaluation
Make informed choices between treatment options based on measures of disease burden such as quality-adjusted life years and disability-adjusted life years
Critique cost-minimization analysis (CMA) in relation to genomic medicine
Critique cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) in relation to genomic medicine
Critique cost-utility analysis (CUA) in relation to genomic medicine
Critique cost-benefit analysis (CBA) in relation to genomic medicine
Acquire and apply knowledge in economic models and human genomics
Evaluate issues around the costs of health interventions
Critique issues around the measurement benefits in healthcare

description: The module introduces key concepts in epidemiology and population and patient level health information.

The module will provide students with an understanding of: 1) why health information is important; 2) how to identify valid sources of health information; 3) health information systems in the UK; and 4) an overview of data governance, digital technologies and quality indicators. It will also provide an introduction to basic concepts in epidemiological methods used to identify and quantify disease and associated risks. Students will be introduced to descriptive epidemiology, measures and comparisons of disease occurrence (incidence, prevalence), and epidemiological study designs: ecological studies, cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, cohort studies, and randomised controlled trials. Students will analyse datasets relevant to each of these five study designs from a range of sources, including, for instance, Census and ONS data; Health Survey for England data; primary care data; and hospital data.

The module will enable students to appreciate the vast amount of accessible health information available, and value the impact of high-quality health intelligence in shaping public health policies and interventions.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the main techniques used to investigate the epidemiology of the important causes of death and ill health
Develop, collate and appraise suitable health information data and systems to describe given health conditions
Identify, interpret and discuss appropriate epidemiological study designs to address population health questions
Summarise, analyse, present and interpret epidemiological and statistical data appropriately
Critically analyse governance structures in handling health information
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of digital technologies in the management of health conditions at a population level

summative: Epidemiology (50%): Written assignment: analysis and reporting of a study dataset using an appropriate epidemiological study design.

Health Information (50%): 2500 word written assignment to investigate the epidemiology of a given health condition, and to critically evaluate aspects of a health information system related to that subject.
Student needs to pass both components (50% or above in each component: Epidemiology and Health Information)

description: Students of this module will learn how to appraise existing evidence about AI health technologies and how to generate local evidence to support decision-making in a specific setting. They will also gain an understanding of the different forms of risk that AI health technologies pose for healthcare providers and the principles and practicalities that influence how those risks are managed.

Best practices in these key areas are emerging, with limited capabilities across many UK and global healthcare providers. Because of the interdisciplinarity and novelty of the challenges posed by AI governance and evaluation in healthcare, this module is accessible for a wide range of applicants. This practice-oriented module is grounded in the faculty's recent or active research in the UK, US and elsewhere. Students will develop competencies that enable them to bring their organisations up to date to efficiently deliver safe, effective and fair AI-enabled healthcare.

Show understanding of the core principles of cyber security, interoperability and clinical risk management relating to clinical AI
Evaluate peer-reviewed evidence of clinical AI performance across the translational pathway
Evaluate local risks and propose mitigations for an AI-enabled healthcare pathway

description: This module will provide students with a strong foundation in anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, contextualised to a clinical setting. This will be accompanied by an introduction to clinical skills, clinical examination techniques and practice, with a strong emphasis on developing professionalism and excellent communication skills.

Clinical experience starts from the earliest stages of the programme as an integral part of the course; thus although the emphasis in this module is predominantly theory, clinical learning forms the major part of the student learning experience, rather than being an adjunct to theoretical learning.

Students will be expected to develop their knowledge of a range of conditions, the available treatment modalities and the process by which clinical decisions (both diagnostic and management) are made. The parameters of the range of conditions students are expected to learn about during the programme, as a whole, are outlined in the `Matrix of Conditions? appended to the national guidance documentation in the `Competence and Curriculum Framework for the Physician Assistant?. data.restrictions:

The two assessments test different elements of the learning outcomes. Both assessments must therefore be passed independently to secure a `pass? for this module.
description: The aim of this module is to introduce students to core concepts and principles which underpin public health as it is practised today. Public Health is a population-based speciality devoted to promoting and protecting health and well-being, preventing ill-health and prolonging life, through the organised efforts of society.1 It consists of three main areas of activity: health improvement, health service quality and health protection. This module will introduce the common principles which underpin all three areas of practice, and then focus on teaching key concepts and approaches to health improvement activities. The module will build on the core knowledge from pre-existing MBChB / BDS undergraduate training, to expose students to the concepts and approaches used in modern-day public health research and practice. Learning will be developed primarily through interactive lectures and expert-led (practitioner, researcher) seminars supported by different forms of enquiry-based and self-directed activities. Students will be expected to undertake preparatory work in relation to each session.
1 Faculty of Public Health definition

description: This module provides additional learning for students who have completed the Global Health module. It is aimed at professionals in public health who may wish to work in resource-poor settings in low and middle-income countries or with Governmental and non-Governmental organisations which operate on a global basis. This module will offer a balance of group work and discussion with the provision of theoretical and applied information in the form of literature and lectures/seminars to enable a firm foundation for addressing a range of topics in relation to low and middle income countries including:
International health targets,
Communicable & non-communicable diseases,
mental health and maternal-child health, healthy ageing and dental health,
lifestyle factors and health promotion
public and private actors in the global policy arena,
health systems delivery and policy,
access to health care,
vulnerable sub-groups, and
ethical considerations of research and health care delivery.

An assessed project will allow the students to develop a policy briefing document on a suitable topic within an identified low or middle income country setting. description: The module takes the planning cycle used in many health care systems as its focus (called the commissioning cycle in UK health services).  It will introduce students to the three key areas of planning, procuring and monitoring health care services.  The module is underpinned by teaching on the critical appraisal of evidence and the use of economic appraisal in health settings.  Particular emphasis is placed on Health Needs Assessment and the ways in which this can be carried out.  Students are exposed in particular to these concepts as they apply to health care delivery.  The module is delivered by a mixture of internal academic experts and external experts experienced in service delivery.

outcomes.outcome: Describe the planning cycle in the context of the provision and funding of health care
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles and practice of health care needs assessment and its application in public health practice
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of economic appraisal of health care
Critically analyse health care policy implementation, in particular through the prioritisation of services and interventions
Demonstrate an understanding of and be able to analyse critical steps in service design or redesign such as service specifications, care pathways and models of care
Evaluate and audit health services to assure and improve quality

reassessment: Resubmission of an amended 2,500 word assignment following individualised feedback.

data.restrictions: Must be a Health care professional with first degree or equivalent, and be a practising clinician or nurse for a minimum of 3 years
description: This module explores scenario writing, the interchangeable role of each member of the simulation faculty, the various simulation technologies that are available and how to `drive? these technologies.
The principles underlying debriefing a healthcare simulation scenario will be explored and different debriefing strategies will be examined.

Teaching for this module takes place over a period of three days; an initial one day of teaching, followed by a block of teaching over two days. A three week break between blocks of teaching has been scheduled to allow students time for reflection and preparation of three a simulation scenarios with learning outcomes in advance of their simulation sessions. The simulation scenarios will be conducted and discussed with peers during the second block of teaching which will take place in the simulation suite.

The module will be offered to students as either CPD or as an accredited module. The students undertaking the accreditation will be registered with the UoB. To be awarded module credits, students undertaking the accredited module will be required to successfully complete all of the module assignments.

Academics within the Institute of Applied Health Research at the UoB will provide academic oversight and teaching support to include quality assurance of course content and second marking of assignments. As such, this module is owned by UoB

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate an understanding of how to create a scenario that is suitable for use in a simulation environment (Simulation scenario with supporting materials)
Demonstrate an understanding of how to run a simulation scenario using faculty members (concurrent learners). (Practical assessment with peers in the simulation suite)

Demonstrate an understanding of and ability to perform each of the required roles in the faculty (scenario lead, faculty plant, manikin `driver?. (Practical assessment with peers in the simulation suite)
Demonstrate an understanding of how to construct an evidence based simulation programme for teaching and learning (Healthcare simulation teaching and learning programme)
Demonstrate an understanding of how to effectively debrief a simulation scenario. (Simulation scenario with supporting materials and healthcare simulation teaching and learning programme).

summative: 1. Development of a simulation scenario with supporting materials (i.e. patient notes, results of blood tests and other investigations) to include a timetable for running the scenario, a debrief, learner evaluation and list of the resources required to run and debrief the scenario with peers in the simulation suite (50%)
2. Practical assessment using scenarios with peers in the simulation suite (pass/fail).

3. A 3000 word healthcare simulation teaching and learning programme, justifying the use of simulation for teaching and learning with reference to the evidence base to include: fully defined simulation scenarios with learning objectives and debrief and a timetable for running the scenario/s (50%)
Students will be expected to pass all elements of the summative assessment to receive an overall pass
reassessment: Students not obtaining a pass on the assessment will be required to resit the failed element and the module mark will be set at 50%

description: The aim of this module is to introduce students to core concepts and principles which underpin health improvement and health promotion as it is practised in England today. Public Health is a population-based activity devoted to promoting and protecting health and well-being, preventing ill-health and prolonging life through the organised efforts of society. It consists of three main areas of activity: health improvement (health promotion), health service quality and health protection. This module will establish the common principles which underpin health promotion practice, and then focus on teaching key concepts and approaches to health improvement activities.

The module will consist of lectures, expert seminars, and small group teaching supported by different forms of enquiry-based learning. Students will be expected to undertake preparatory work in relation to each session.   The module will enable students to analyse, critically, health promotion and improvement policy, research, methods and strategies and to become familiar with the principles of the design, implementation and evaluation of interventions to improve population health.

outcomes.outcome: To discuss critically the health improvement and promotion policy, theories and research which underpin delivery of present-day health improvement activities
To consider and to evaluate health improvement and promotion priorities, strategies and methods used with individuals, groups, partnerships and communities
To analyse critically issues of power, ethics and politics within health improvement and health promotion policy and practice
To demonstrate the ability to manage their own learning, and to make critical use of relevant resources.

summative: One structured written proposal (max 2000 words) critically and succinctly describing the development, implementation and evaluation of a specified activity to improve health within a defined population
reassessment: Resubmission of failed assessment following individualised support, feedback and guidance.

sameLevelModule.title: LI Health Improvement
description: Health improvement is defined as the process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants, and thereby improve their health. It is central to the work of public health practitioners. This module will enable students to critically analyse health improvement policy, research, methods and strategies at a regional, national and international scale.

The module will consider the scope of health improvement and promotion; health promotion theories, models and strategies; changing behaviour; patient and public participation in health improvement; collaboration, partnerships, joint working and community development; ethics, ideology, power and politics relevant to health improvement; and the commissioning, planning and evaluation of health improvement and health promotion.

outcomes.outcome: Understand the breadth of health improvement activity and describe this in terms of individuals, groups, communities and regions/countries.
Understand and be able to discuss key theories and research that underpin evidence based approaches to health improvement.
Propose health improvement priorities at all levels (local, regional, national and international), and be able to critically discuss strategies and methods to address these.
Understand the principles of evaluating health improvement strategies, policies and activities, and demonstrate how to apply these in practice.
Understand how issues of power, ethics and politics influence health improvement strategies, policy and practice.

summative: Individual written assignment - 3,000 word proposal for or critical analysis of a health improvement problem or strategy
The pass mark for the module is 40%
reassessment: One opportunity to resubmit the written assignment.

description: This module explores definitions and drivers 'health inequalities' and 'health disparities' so that there is a clear understanding of their meaning and causes. It illustrates the different ways that health inequalities and disparities manifest, including differences in life expectancy, prevalence of chronic diseases, access to healthcare services, and overall quality of life. Disadvantaged groups, including those facing poverty, discrimination, or marginalized social status, tend to experience higher rates of illness, disability, and premature death. A critical perspective on disadvantage is encouraged that accounts for intersectionality and sensitivity to context. Examples are provided of evidence-based actions and interventions that can be incorporated and implemented into everyday practice to address health inequalities and disparities. This includes consideration of organisations who need to work together to address health disparities and health inequalities, including the public, private, and third sector.

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a broad understanding of what is meant by `health inequalities? `health disparities?
Integrate and synthesise evidence on the underlying causes of health inequalities and health disparities
Identify original opportunities to implement evidence-based actions and interventions to address health inequalities and health disparities
Reflect critically on organisations that need to work together address health disparities and health inequalities
Project planning of original and sustainable initiatives and interventions to address health inequalities and disparities

summative: One structured 2500-word essay (90%) and 10-minute presentation (10%). The essay structure follows the learning outcomes and group-based tutorials - students will identify an opportunity to address health inequalities and/or inequities by integrating and synthesising evidence, reflect critically on the organisations that need to be involved, and create and present an actionable project plan

description: The module introduces students to population level health information and to principles of health informatics.

The aim of the module is to provide students with an understanding of: why health information is important; how to identify valid sources of health information; health information system in UK and how they are integrated; the governance structure behind health information; the role of computerised decision support systems; and emerging information related technologies in delivering health care.

The module enables students to: appreciate the vast amount of accessible health information available; value the impact of high-quality health intelligence in shaping public health policies and interventions and understand the role of health informatics in delivering health care in an efficient way.

outcomes.outcome: Develop, collate and appraise suitable health information data and systems to describe given health conditions;
Understand and interpret current trends and future developments in population health data collection and storage;
Critically analyse governance structures in handling health information related data;
Understand the principles of the role of computerised decision support tools in the management of health conditions at a population level.

summative: One 2500 word written assignment to investigate the epidemiology of a given health condition and analyse aspects of a health information system related to that subject

data.title: LM Health Management and Leadership Research Project
description: This module aims to equip students with skills needed to conceive, design and conduct a feasible piece of research in the field of health management and leadership suitable for publication within a relevant journal.
Students will experience data collection, management and analysis, prior to writing up in the form of an academic paper or dissertation.

Project supervisors will be allocated in consultation with the module co-ordinator.  Students will meet with their supervisor(s) in Semester 1 to develop a research proposal for the project to be carried out in Semester 2, with further supervisory meetings throughout.    If necessary, ethical approval for the proposed project will be obtained and scoping work (e.g. familiarisation with local policy and practice) undertaken.

The module is delivered across the first and second semesters.  There will be group contact time and teaching in the first semester will involve lectures and seminars where students will meet to discuss project ideas and development. Towards the end of Semester 1, each student will give an oral presentation (summative assessment - 10% of module) of the research proposal to the group, submitting a written research proposal for formative assessment.  They will also make submissions to the Internal Research Ethics Committee as appropriate for their chosen project.

In Semester 2 students will work under close supervision to conduct their research project.  Students will have tutorials with their supervisor on a regular basis and these will identify problems with data collection, monitor progress and support data management and delivery, enabling the student to fully engage with the research process from concept to completion.  Students will also have access to statistics and research skills clinics throughout both semesters to supplement supervision.

Towards the end of Semester 2 students will present an academic poster of their research findings (summative assessment ? 15% of module) and will also submit their project write up either as a dissertation or academic paper written in the style of an appropriate journal (summative assessment ? 75% of module).

outcomes.outcome: Demonstrate a sound, broad and detailed understanding of an issue relating to health management and leadership
Carrying out and and reporting a piece of research in health management and leadership which is scientifically valid and practically manageable within the given time frame.
Apply critically the generic knowledge and skills gained during the taught elements of the programme
Demonstrate an understanding of the research ethical approval process, obtaining any necessary research ethical approval for the proposed project
Contribute constructively to a discussion of their own and others research ideas and protocols.

summative: Assessment of project comprising three elements:
10% - academic poster summarising key research findings/experiences75% - dissertation or academic paper written in the style of an appropriate journal.
